en: The *Āryā-saptaśatī* composed by Govardhanācārya. May there be prosperity!
Victorious is the body of the Lord, adorned with ashes and bristling with horripilation at the grasping of the hand;
for even though he remains as nothing but ash, the God of Love has, as it were, sprouted anew within him.
"Do not vomit; swallow this poison," thus was he told with anxiety by his grandfather.
In the morning, Śambhu conquers, full of shame, his lips soiled with collyrium.

Victorious is the Enemy of Smara, who wears a necklace of poison at the feet of his beloved; he appears like one entering for refuge into the presence of the God of Love, who wields uneven arrows, with a sword fastened to his neck.
Victorious is the side-glance from the forehead of the moon-crested Lord, thick with lashes, as his beloved bows before him;
it is like a thorny ketaka arrow placed upon Cupid’s bow by the God of Love.

Victorious is this lotus-face of Śambhu, which has the matted locks for its filaments, the Gaṅgā for its nectar, the circle of skulls for its seed-vessel, and which is born from the mud of the poison in his throat.
Victorious is Śiva, whose mind is fixed on the face of Gaurī and who, unaware that even his cupped hands of twilight water are being drunk by the serpent upon his bracelet, is laughed at by Vijayā.

Victorious is the handful of water offered by Śambhu from his lotus-hand, which fell as it slipped from fingers loosened by the trembling of beholding the face of Gaurī reflected therein, and which was being filled with a profusion of perspiration.

Victory to Śiva, whose moon is sweetened by the twilight-like persistence of the red lac from the feet of his beloved who is angry in love, and whose neck is like a touchstone for the gold of her bangles.
Victorious is the moon of Pūrṇa’s nails, doubled by the anklets and bound by the chains of love,
upon the crescent moon of Śiva on the toes, middle parts, and ankles of Gaurī’s feet.
May the eye of the lotus-eyed Lord, covered by his glorious hand, grant you happiness—
that eye which, resembling a lotus, seems to have come through the cavity of the navel as if to gaze upon his own hip.
Victorious is the dark chest of the enemy of Mura, tawny with the saffron from Śrī’s breasts,
which it adorns like the sun Kaustubha adorning the sky at the break of day.
Victorious is the chest of the Slayer of Madhu, which bears the reflection of his beloved’s body along with the Kaustubha gem;
beholding it, Lakṣmī practices the role of the man, as if looking into a mirror.

Victorious is that foot of the Enemy of Mura, from which Lakṣmī emerges with her fingers playfully extended from the navel— the very foot by which the Fortune of the Lotus-navelled One was made worthy of Him.
May the line of hair on Murāri’s chest, its upper portion graced by the Śrīvatsa mark,
remove your fever like the shadow of a lotus with an upturned stalk from the navel.
Victorious is Hari, whose head is that of a horse; singing sweetly in a manner befitting a horse’s face, he holds the three Vedas like a lute with seven strings appropriate for a sacrifice.
Victorious is he, O mighty-armed one, by whom the earth— though long submerged within the belly of the ocean—
was forcibly lifted up along with the hosts of serpents as if they were his own entrails.
I bow to Janārdana, who is the potter of the cosmic egg and who has the form of a serpent;
upon the vast circle of whose hoods the earth bears the beauty of a shallow earthen bowl.
Victorious is the shank of Caṇḍī, which, when her beloved touches it with his head,
acts like a pillar of victory for the God of Love, who has conquered everyone down to Śaṅkara.
Victorious is that face of the Mountain’s Daughter, which makes even Śambhu appear like a lotus with its stalk as its navel, as he assumes the role of the man in her embrace.

Victory to the breasts of the Daughter of the Snowy Mountain, which were seized by Bāhuleya— who was filled with the suspicion that they were the face of Gajāsya hidden within her lap— and which were then touched by the hand of Hara with a smile.
Victorious is that Caṇḍī, before whose feet Candraśikha fell, though he was worthy of her neck, yet was repelled by a mere grunt like an arrow of Love.

Victorious is Lakṣmī, whose glance is averted by modesty and who is laughed at by gods and demons, as she assumes the form of Kaiṭabhī while wearing the garland of choice offered by the God, though she is full of guile.
I bow to those Asuras and to Hari himself, who assumed the deceptive form of Kaiṭabhī;
for they, greedy for the honey of her bimba-like lips, abandoned even the nectar of immortality.

Victorious is the sport of Lakṣmī, who is blinded by passion: she has made the serpent her couch, disregards Garuḍa, strikes the Creator with her necklace, and drinks his breath with her hundred hoods.
Victorious is the meditation on Kaiṭabha by Kamalā as she assumes the role of the man; for she was gazed upon with longing by this smiling Hari, who understood the expression of her form.
Victorious is the Creator, who sleeps upon the lotus of his navel, lulled by the sprinkling of the cool breaths of Śrī while she indulges in the curiosity of amorous play,
as the humming of her outspread bee-like eyebrows resounds.
Victory to you, who have one tusk, two mothers, are beyond the three qualities (*guṇas*), and though four-armed, possess five hands;
you who are praised by the six-faced one, whose body is the eighth son of the fragrance of the seven-leaved tree.
Worship Gajavaktra (the Elephant-faced One) with sincere devotion, using two auspicious jars as a vessel;
for upon his trunk, which wavers with the water of his ichor, bees hang like sesame seeds.
By those [powers] by which the bodiless one was made possessed of a body and women were made no longer women,
he [the Buddha] has caused both desire and the desirous woman to bow down, inclined toward his left foot.
I bow to the poet born from the anthill, whose face is adorned with many ornaments and radiant with rows of diverse colors, like the rainbow of Indra.
I bow to the *Bhārata*, the essence and the refined extract of Vyāsa’s words,
by which the Goddess of Speech bears her very name as an ornament.
When the *Rāmāyaṇa*, which brings glory to the lineage of Kakutstha, exists, what need is there for anything else? When the Ganges flows with its many flavors, does a small canal ever flourish?
Alas! Because of the fault of his excessively long life, Vyāsa’s fame was lost;
yet who would not say that he is the very same person, now rich in virtues, having entered another birth?
We pay homage to the poets of the Śrī-Rāmāyaṇa, the Mahābhārata, and the Bṛhatkathā,
by whom the eloquent Sarasvatī flows forth divided, like the triple-streamed Gaṅgā.
Even at the time of instruction, the verses of Kālidāsa— abounding in the cooing of playful women with intentional, sweet, and tender voices— are for the sake of delight.
Through its connection with Bhavabhūti, the very earth—though it supports all beings—shines forth as the goddess of speech;
otherwise, why would even a stone weep at his compassion?
I understand that just as Śikhaṇḍinī was born previously,
so too did Vāṇī become Bāṇa in order to attain greater boldness.
I pay homage to my father Nīlāmbara, who, following his guru, counts those whose religious duties have become contracted as nothing at all— just like the poet Uśanas.
The King, the ornament of the Sena dynasty, alone is capable of fashioning all the arts of composition and the moon; so too is the full-moon night.

In poetry, words that possess a friendly rapport with the syllables— being neither harsh nor vulgar— and men who likewise possess a friendly rapport with their letters— being neither cruel nor base— are both truly refined (*sādhu*) for the purpose of conveying meaning.
Just as a wood-worm does not enter timber saturated with resin, a fault does not take root in the mind of the virtuous which is steeped in aesthetic flavor (*rasa*);
yet, one who is full of many faults does not even accept that flavor, like a person afflicted by a derangement of the humors (*sannipāta*).
Even a poem devoid of merit is relished when it reaches the mouths of the virtuous;
even a mere hiss, when blown through a fine reed, captivates the ear.
Though he himself possesses many flaws and spreads fickleness in every direction,
the malicious person is nonetheless appointed as the sieve for winnowing out faults from the chaff.

Neither in a literary composition nor in a river that fails to reveal its hidden meanings and lacks clarity does there exist any aesthetic flavor (*rasa*) for the gratification of those who possess discernment of *rasa*.

We consider that poetry— which is not to be cultivated by the wicked, which is like nectar, possesses the arrangement of gold, and consists of a multitude of beautiful meanings— to be equal to heaven itself.

Satiated by the cooking of the finest rice-grains of words, winnowed by the winnowing-basket of the tongues of true poets, one no longer values even the lip of one's beloved; what then of nectar, which is but a slave?
A well-spoken word, though it may contain stumbling steps and lack the ornamentation of polished sound,
delights like a woman going to meet her lover, for it possesses the excellence of erotic passion.
On the road, poetry—intent on grasping words—neither delights the heart nor the ear;
it is like an anklet in the assembly of connoisseurs, or during a time of play.
Only for one who has tasted the nectar-like essence of a beloved’s lips are sweet utterances produced;
a cuckoo does not warble its melodious notes unless it has experienced the flavor of a mango bud.

The young poets study the *bhāva* (emotional state) as it is strung together by the side-glances of young girls, commented upon by the third part of the eyes of unchaste women, and explained by female messengers.

The Āryā verses of Govardhana are smooth in their metrical flow and lyrical movement, enchanting like women who visit the hearts of the virtuous; they are full of aesthetic flavor, transparent, and the secret essence of non-dual passion.
Speech, though naturally endowed with the aesthetic flavor appropriate to Prakrit, was forcibly elevated to Sanskrit,
just as the daughter of Kalinda (the Yamunā), whose waters follow the low-lying terrain, reaches the surface of the sky.
Those for whom this *Āryā-saptaśatī* is disregarded by those of bold minds do not enter the hearts of amorous women, as if they were without a female messenger (*dūtī*).

Like a beloved woman who has cast off her fine garments, speech that is devoid of *rasa*— even if it is pure and adorned with ornaments— does not please the mind, just as a stone statue (*śālabhañjī*) fails to delight even if it is beautifully decorated.
Thus ends the section on the commencement of the work. The Section on the Letter *A*:
May the wives of travelers live on for as many days as remain until their destination; be gracious!
O guardian of the water-shed, cover your breasts, which are like mountains on a path difficult to traverse!
Exceedingly affectionate, virtuous, clever in service, and pleasing to the mind,
she became a humble housewife as soon as her co-wife’s breasts began to swell.

O Kāverī, you who are noisy with waves of wicked character that uproot the *nicula* trees on your banks, you will before long become nothing but the dregs of the mud and the remains of food left by cranes.
O messenger, you who bring the moon in your hand to compose such various words—
where indeed will you be seen on days of calamity?
Let there be withering; let the world point out your blemish; let your vigor be diminished—nevertheless, he will not abandon you, just as the moon does not abandon the shadow of the earth.
Displaying excessive fickleness while penetrating deep within, you— who are exceedingly hard—
make this woman of virtuous conduct noisy yourself, like a stake with a bell.
The flow of passion reaches its peak within the limbs of the young Khañjana couple;
yet their dalliance does not occur upon the surface of the earth where a treasure lies hidden within.
Resorting to blindness at the time of blindness and deafness at the time of deafness,
the Lord of Creatures (Prajāpati) dwelling in the navel is the beloved friend of Śrī and Keśava.
O author of the treasury! It is indeed your gain that you have not torn open the forest-dwellers to examine their bellies while singing their praises in their presence.
Her passion for you disregards her own greatness, transgresses her elders, is indifferent to wealth, defies her infant child, brings her undesired infamy, and is reckless even of her life.
This fabrication of your deceitful words pains me more than my offense;
the blow of a weapon does not cause such agony as the piercing of a needle.
Whatever exists within the mind is reflected in the mirror of an unchaste woman's eyes;
even the eye of Sarasvatī herself perceives it not, as if obscured by a film of darkness.
That which is slander when uttered by another's mouth is the very same thing that is called humor when spoken from a beloved's mouth;
that which is smoke produced from other fuel is the very same thing that is called incense when produced from agallochum.
O fortunate one, wandering about, agitated by curiosity and following the scent,
this poor girl has fallen into delusion upon you, like a bee upon a poisonous flower.
O, merely by the suspicion that he is a charmingly scented elephant, other elephants are crushed;
here, my elephants are nothing but mere insects who consume only female elephants.
The young bride, her body dwarfed by excessive discipline, does not even cross the threshold of the house;
yet the saffron field knows her bold display of prowess.
What is the use of internal qualities if even two or three witnesses for them are rare?
That quality of song is such that it captivates even the forest-dwelling deer.
Having first seen the young woman joyful in the morning because all her ornaments were disarrayed,
and then seeing the red lac-dye on the head of her beloved, the co-wives sighed deeply.
O modest one, whose limbs are exhausted from intense passion at the dead of night, you who sleep so blissfully:
open the petals of your lotus-eyes; a beautiful dawn has come for you.
With her face unblemished and her breasts untouched, and with her hips and thighs held far away,
she embraced me with her arms only under a hundred oaths.
O slender-limbed one, this view of yours, so highly honored and capable of transcending the sacred scriptures—
like the established doctrine of the Jinas accompanied by its latent impressions (vāsanā), whom does it not delude?

For so long a time, this woman, whose virtues as a new-found lover have only recently become familiar to her, has grieved for herself— deceived by fear and shame regarding an improper object— and has not spoken to her bed-fellows.
With her limbs seized by a fierce separation from you that persists through passion,
she remains with only half her body left, like Gaurī, whose excellent form was reduced to a single half by the Enemy of Tripura.

O friend, when a lover is inclined toward another and acts contrary [to one's wishes], those women who place their hopes in him like [rivers following] a current, desiring his path, become objects of ridicule with their efforts rendered fruitless.
He who is dearer than all that is dear, dwelling eternally in the heart— that very soul rolls about in separation, just as you do when in union with her at her throat.
O beloved, there is no such agony when you are out of sight as when you are visible yet unattainable;
the sun-stone merely withers at night and blazes only during the day.
Invisible even to a friend, yet gladdening by his mere presence, this beloved one is to be enjoyed in secret under some pretext, like wealth in a kingless land.
"You have heard of my transgressions; tell me the truth, looking into my face—if that rogue whose mouth steals away my pride does not speak."
As the two youths follow one another along the current, moving from bank to bank,
their *māgha* bath is not completed even when the sun has risen.
O mango creeper, whose limbs are bent by the weight of fruit and who possesses a fragrance blooming in all directions— you,
though indeed laden with fruit, are truly as if fruitless, marked as you are by the pots and shards of outcaste scavengers.
The world offered its salutation with palms joined, and the earth was colored red without even reaching a state of withering;
O friend, even a very brief dwelling at twilight leads only to happiness.
"Alas, my friends have gone away, leaving me behind while disregarding my lack of compliance!
If you act so forcefully toward me, today I shall cast off my body upon you."
"You are one whose passion is unstable, a gambler, proud, and fickle—a mere jester.
I shall see how you become upright when you fall into the hand of my friend."
This gaze of yours— merciless, with a timid mind, showing no compassion, and unrestrained— pursues you even as you turn away, like the Ganges following Bhagīratha.

O woman of excellent complexion, even though I am looking up at you, no satisfaction has been granted by you, who are like the spout of a water-pitcher whose flow of nectar is stilled by internal turbidity.
O simple one, for a moment, the mutual exchange of charming fragrances between the straight trunk of the *sarala* tree and the temples of the elephant, delighted by rut, proclaims their encounter.
Her gaze, emerging clearly from the edge of the curtain torn by her fingernails,
flows like a stream of nectar— pure and stainless as it passes through the opening in the cloth.
As she departs for her husband’s house, her mother makes the path slippery with tears;
yet she, proud of her virtues, laughs softly with a face that has been weeping dryly.
When, as she rests her head upon my lap with eyes half-closed, softly murmuring "cruel one," when shall I loosen the knot of her braid with my nails anointed with fragrant oil?
O you who are naturally beautiful without ornaments, your jewelry is an object of ridicule for others;
you are like a flower on a forest tree to the barren creepers.
Even those who are ignorant and unable to move have attained the supreme state by some means;
they are celebrated by people as "ministers," like pills of the power of policy.
In this world, our friend possesses a nature cool with excessive virtue and a mild majesty;
yet her beloved knows her majesty when he is scorched by her momentary perversity.
Even regarding other women, by meditating on them as his wife, he attains his desire,
just as one beholding stone images as being deities.
O child, by not humbling yourself before this love that is profound and sweet on all sides, you do not become its vessel, just like the water of a river [that does not remain] at the bottom.
The ketaka bud, by its very nature, deserves to be placed upon the heads of young men; it requires no stringing together and does not depend on the path of [artificial] qualities.
O fortunate one, she wears that garland— which removes all her fever and was placed upon her by your own hand— as the medicine for the burning heat of the nights spent on her husband’s bed.
O Sundara, by means of your conduct— which is indifferent even toward its own immeasurable virtues—
you have made her, who has no other resort, like a ship caught in a whirlpool.
Moreover, because your beloved Rāmā has placed her upper garment upon you so that you might return,
even though you are clad in but a single cloth, your splendor exceeds that of all the young men.
One half of me breathes while the other is dead, as if I were the one whose body was embraced by the nectar-like beloved upon meeting on the road, yet only half of him.
Though ignored by my beloved, who was indifferent to my greatness under the pretext of sleep,
I, a fickle man, was awakened by the bed which had become as hard as a stone due to the tears held within it.
O traveler, for you who have tasted sugar merely because of the similarity of its sound,
the cutting of your tongue will be slight, but the public ridicule ahead of you will be great.
Although her pride is being struck down by people who are difficult to overcome due to their fresh youth,
the housewife still maintains the intoxication of her good fortune because her son is dear to his father.
As if humiliated now by the powerful summer heat,
the feeble cold enters the water held within the jar-like breasts of young women eager for their bath.
He lulls my entire body to rest, releases my eyes from distress, and steals away [all other thought];
like sleep itself, my beloved does not allow me to leave his bed.
Your body— with hands resting on your shoulders, grasping your hair, with white nail-marks still wet from the consecration,
and with lips and eyes washed clean— is the sharpened weapon of the Bodiless One.
Among the clear young men, the beautiful-eyed courtesans display their unrestrained hearts as if they were placed within them, just as a face is reflected in the surfaces of mirrors.
Out of excessive bashfulness, you yourself have made manifest your beloved, even though he was hidden,
just as the Vaijayantī banner atop a palace reveals its peak as it billows above.
By means of the cord of mutual entanglement, cows, through many placements of their hooves,
gore even a wicked threshing-post that stands in the middle, having taken hold of it.
A slanderer does not cause such pain with his harsh cries as he does through his failure to offer favor;
a mosquito causes more distress by buzzing in the ear than by sucking blood.
First there is lightness, which is subsequently concealed by greatness, yet not by its majesty;
thus do those who know the ten incarnations call the Trivikrama incarnation "Vāmana."
The suckling at your breast is on your lap, your servant is at your feet, and your beloved is behind you;
O housewife, what more could possibly be desired when you suspect even a child?
The lower lip was raised, a cooing sound made, the eyes were closed, and the head was shaken;
even without physical contact, the young couple seemed to have attained the bliss of a kiss.
In my excessive haste, this arm was thrust through a gap in the fence into the house;
now, thrilled by the touch of my beloved, it will not return by that same path.
Beholding this exceedingly tremulous and weighty slope of your hips, situated in the midst of your garment like a fresh cloud in the sky, I am not satiated, O Cātaka-like one.

This tortoise, whose face is the lofty eastern mountain, vomits forth the blood of twilight, being weighed down by the burden of the earth which is itself oppressed by the weight of the elephant of darkness.
The dull-witted person dwells within that which is dull, like a deer in the cool-rayed moon;
but he who is not dull-witted, though entered into the sun, emerges from it as if it were the moon.
Disregarding public scandal, this wretched girl, trembling with the joy of touching your hand,
prepares a bed for the fever that is about to arrive.

Behold how two things born of the same lineage—one possessing fullness and the other insignificance—become respectively the string and the bow; one becomes the subordinate accessory, while the other is the master.
Exhausted by fresh amorous play, the young woman gradually wipes away her perspiration,
just as the springtime, when bent low to string its bow, dries the honey from the flower-arrowed god’s vine-like bow.
When a neighbor who is of noble birth, steadfast, mature, and full of passion develops an attachment [to one], then I consider the bliss of Brahman to be no more than a blade of grass.
This body of yours, with tears falling incessantly, pale yet tender,
brings me relief from the agony of the burning of Love’s arrows, like clarified butter washed a hundred times.
The field, beautiful with strings of guñjā berries fallen within it,
shines as if its heart were rent asunder by the grief of losing the modesty of its own cowherd girls.
"This was struck by him! This was struck!"—weeping thus, the wife, her modesty shattered under the pretext of anger, displays every limb of her body before her husband for the neighbor to see.
Thus ends the Section on the Letter ‘A’, accompanied by the Vibhāvya commentary. Now begins the Section on the Letter ‘Ā’:
Indeed, in order to manifest the aesthetic flavor (*rasa*) in its entirety, both internally and externally, [the poet] must constantly [strive].
One knows three things: a non-existent thing, the eloquent verse of a true poet, and a glass jar.
O proud woman, you turn your face away from light itself on certain days and do not remain to its south;
yet even so, like a shadow, you alone take away my heat.
Her commands, her plaintive intonations, her requests, her rebukes, her laughter, and her dry weeping—
contemplating such mastery in the art of love-making, I am not satiated with her.
"You shall command; you shall place your foot upon the head of your beloved—why do you hasten?
O charming girl who values the wrong moment, do not let love, whose sprouts have just begun to grow, be broken."
"Having suffered defeat in this game where the stake was set at a playful sport,
take away the dice!"— thus the friends were sent away under a pretext of feigned anger.
O friend, you have been placed upon the head by that great man because of your adorable qualities;
yet this fault of yours—your wavering—is like that of a banner atop a palace.
O fair-limbed one, having cast off even this moist garment from your breasts and hips,
your cloth now drinks in the rays of the sun as if to reach you who are situated in the sky.
Though placed upon a stone with the mantra,
"May you become like a stone," she laughed at the sight of her lover's face even while submerged during the calamity of the wedding ceremony.
She comes and goes, she causes weariness, and like a female bee she steals away the honey;
you alone are the presiding deity of my mind, as Śrī is to the lotus.
Having reached the southern direction, the sun leaves the northern one without delay;
for it is generally those women who are truly "southern" (courteous) who captivate a man.

Some [women] remove the torment of poison through the application of substances taken by mouth or as ointments; yet another, like a certain medicinal creeper, brings life back even while remaining seated in the assembly.
Do you remember her with her hair swaying in the movement, the multitude of her moving girdle-bells tinkling, acting the part of the man, like the handle of the fly-whisk for the God of Love?
"You insult Karṇa with your eye, yet even Bali was bound by you threefold at his waist"—
O fair-limbed one, you who have conquered all generous givers, do you feel shame when it comes to the gift of your own body?
Agitated by the playful curiosity of tossing, kicking, leaping over, and seizing the hair,
the slender-limbed woman was not made to hear the religious precept that even a husband is a venerable teacher for women.
He has come without looking back, like a beggar seeking a cowrie shell;
by him, who is unable even to carry his own loincloth, I have been robbed.

This is the reclining posture of the fair-limbed maiden: with one leg drawn up, her upper thigh slightly covered and the other half-thigh concealed, her chest heaving with breath, and her navel clearly visible as she moves in her sleep.
O fortunate one, by giving you your garment while taking back no small amount of wealth,
the foolish washerwoman’s mistress has been rendered penniless in just a few days.
Let it be; better that the betel-nut tree be barren—do not cultivate it for the sake of its yield.
From this very tree, even when it bears fruit, you shall experience only distress.
When the gods, having placed the double-tongued serpent in their own hands, began the churning of the ocean,
it was only fitting that its result should have been nothing other than the terrible poison.
I remember her bed, where her locks of hair were disheveled, one arm rested upon a breast trembling with sighs, and her garment was loose as her body was rendered helpless by passion.
O fair-limbed one, this mango sprout, with its reddish-dark luster, has emerged from the seed;
it shines forth, having risen upward as if from the shell of a young tortoise.
The beloved’s gaze— unwavering at its corners, rich in many virtues, and bestowing long-lasting delight—
draws my mind away, just as a fishhook and line pulls a fish from a lake.
Speak as you wish, O gambler; what do you have to hide from me? This friend of mine, a wretch of life, bears the very mark of the female species, O fortunate one!
Alas, you have been tasted out of delusion; indeed, the sweetness of your face was known to me. Yet you, like a razor smeared with honey, know only how to cut the tongue.
O fortunate one, by what blessed man may your lotus-stalk arm— naturally delicate yet with its bracelet broken by his pull— be grasped, as if it were the very kingdom of Love?
Having ascended far, disregarding fierce afflictions, and revealing yourself,
O fair-limbed one, you carry me away like a boat with a sail catching the wind.
Exertion and the harming of others—this is your essence, O dog of the hunter!
Having driven you away, this deer may now be divided among others.
Even though it is not yet fully ripened, the paddy plant, agitated by the swaying of its rows, draws in the young traveler here as if leading his own self toward him,
like a deer.
When it was still moist, what could it have said even when struck? Now, O friend, out of its hardened state, it rattles harshly like a drum.
I am her obedient servant, enduring both her blows and her insults; indeed, I am hers, yet she—cool as the moon in her virtue—does not even know how to speak anything other than what is pleasing.
Having placed the churning stick in the milk-jar, the cowherd girl, her vine-like arms exhausted and failing to reach the *pārijāta* tree, casts the blame for the fault upon fate.

Let alone her pride or her speaking to her friends; having confessed her misconduct even to me, that slender-limbed girl, her pride in the excellence of her charms now slackened, was herself filled with shame.
Bearing the beauty of refreshment through her whirlpools white with foam,
the river Surasā, her waters resonant with song, sings the auspicious hymn for union with her beloved.
Thus ends the section on the letter *ā*, accompanied by the Vibhāvya commentary. Now begins the section on the letter *i*:
This [woman], removing her upward gaze and casting a contraction of her eyes before me—
We do not know what this day-sleep, like a co-wife, says to you.

Cupid, out of curiosity, takes refuge in the body of this young girl— which is like a bow with pellets— as a single bud-like breast nestled within the string of a pearl necklace stretched across both walls of her bosom.
Look, here on this tree-deer hanging from the peak of a mountain, its body trembling with playful fear,
a female bird desires to fly down out of delusion that it is her own nest.
O fair-limbed one, the flow of the sugarcane river, the game of dice, the seizing of pride,
and this creeper-like brow of yours— each brings a greater relish when broken.
"O friend, tell me, what evil deed have you committed— like a shadow— to wander away from him as he turns his face toward you, avoiding you like a serpent?"
O deer, why do you place your trust in her whose eyes flicker with feigned curiosity?
This hunter’s wife, agitated by impetuosity, is lashing her tail at you.
This earth, adorned by the great ocean, carries much pride of self-importance;
yet even its entire back cannot encompass the shell of the Lord in his tortoise form.
Thus ends the section on the letter *i*, accompanied by the commentary *Vibhāvākhyā*. The section on the letter *ī*:
He, burning with jealousy and anger as he contemplated union with his own wife, [thought] of her...
I am extinguished by the intense bliss arising from the meditation on the hips and the garment fallen [from them].
O bee, why do you fall fruitlessly upon this [plant], deluded by the thought that it is fit to be possessed by a lord?
This worthless sprout of a rogue is devoid of nectar, though its name suggests gold.
As soon as the winter has passed, its dullness only slightly remaining, the slender pond is enjoyed intensely by the limbs for a long time, like a young woman in the bloom of fresh youth.
Thus ends the section on the letter *ī*, accompanied by the commentary *Vibhāvya*. Now begins the section on the letter *u*:
"O lady of radiant limbs, by your broad eye, which has the bow of your arched eyebrows as its string..."
Even those who are immovable are not truly great if they have been brought to a state of instability.
O friend, let that unique Mount Mandara alone bear the weight of dignity, for it was upon its slope that the gods, having brought Śrī, suspended the serpent as a lofty pillar.
This moon, the source of nectar, shines forth raining down moonlight with its mark made manifest;
it is like the cart [of Rohiṇī], which, having its axle stuck in the foot of Kṛṣṇa, has begun to pour out milk.
Those conciliatory advances of the gambler were overlooked by you at the word of your friend;
now, even if he speaks harshly under the pretext of a quarrel, I shall depart.
O bashful one, who has not perceived your cleverness in the role reversal at dawn, when you turned your string of pearls into a sacred thread?
O young woman, this flight of birds soaring from the palace flutters like a Vaijayantī banner torn and scattered by the wind.
O golden *ketakī*, let not your abundance of fragrance unfold while the swarms of bees are obstructed by your jagged petals, which have been kept awake and bewildered.
With your brow arched, O waveless-eyed one, why do you brood over what is past? The ripening of love is as bitter as that of treacle when subjected to a slight mishap.
As her friend was departing for the sake of [her lover], she, whose brow was curved with feigned anger,
snatched away her ear-ornament in such a way that it fell like a struck lamp.
Even when risen at the edge of the sky, the sun does not shine brightly amidst the dense mass of frost,
like a lamp placed upon the rim of a shallow bowl filled with solidified ghee.
In rising, sitting down, lying down, turning over, twisting, and moving about,
my beloved— who clings to my heart— constantly deludes me like a persistent breath.
Between the two youths— one terrified by the god of love manifesting through the pride of lost fortune,
and the other whose mind remains inscrutable— a single glance serves as a messenger entrusted with a mission.
Her body, its hips motionless due to contact with the most excellent lover,
is dragged here and there by the gods like Mount Mandara.
Having brought a *kuḍava* measure of *kalama* rice, the fearful plowman tells the physician that a red disease, resembling the crescent moon, has arisen on the breast of his daughter-in-law.
With your lips half-open like buds and your eyes half-closed in fear of the particles of ash, even the smoke does not linger here; cease, for this is merely a bee following your breath.
O my wife, this tress of mine floats above like a row of swans;
yet you, having reached my heart, dwell there like a lotus stalk in a lake.
The thief, his hand slipped from the sleeve of his arm which was slick with sweat and trembling,
prays for the welfare of your two firm breasts, O fair-limbed one, which are like the hem of a five-fold garment.
O mango bud, as you are being pulled by my friend— who has raised her arms, revealing the base of her shoulders—
your attainment of a most exalted position shines forth.
O young woman, your necklace— placed upon the jar-like breasts that rise high, its ends clinging to your hips, and resembling a wooden beam spanning a very deep chasm— agitates my heart.
In the vicinity of the crescent moon, which is like the cool-rayed one brought to life,
the clusters of stars shimmer like drops of nectar falling from the bow held by the flower-armed god.
Having brought my beloved to me and removed my burning pride— which was unaware of the improper time—
you have set forth like a messenger, O Night, at the very commencement of our dalliance.
Having you as your sole resort, O most excellent woman, you take away your friend’s fortitude— just as an elephant, having attacked the water of a lake with his trunk, takes it away by touching it.
Thus ends the Section on the Letter *U*, accompanied by its commentary.
**The Section on the Letter *Ū*** "Carry her away on your back for a long time, even though she is immovable and clings to you."
O All-Enduring One, why do you embrace the tortoise with its hard shell?
Thus ends the section on the letter *ū*, accompanied by the commentary *Vibhāvya*.
**The Section on the Letter *ṛ*** Place your feet straightly; O friend, avoid all the conduct of city-dwellers.
In this place, the lord of the village is a ḍākinī who punishes even for a mere sidelong glance.
"Having heard that the Bull is being sung here, we, who have mastered the musical notes, have arrived;
for who would not show great respect toward this cow-pen when it is established for the peace of the cattle?"

Thus ends the section on the letter *ṛ*, accompanied by the commentary *Vibhāvya*. **The Section on the Letter *e*:** Hara alone knows the excellence of his beloved’s lower lip; the other gods are fools.
He who, perceiving poison and nectar as equal, drank only the venom.
"That he might not come back again"—this was the inauspicious thought I harbored regarding his departure;
now that very same thought is the reason for the master of the burnt house remaining here.
O fortunate one, as she leaps over each young man like a flickering glance skipping from pebble to pebble,
her trembling finger comes to rest upon you, as if it has reached Mount Meru.
He alone truly lives, Rāhu, who, though his own heart is empty, is possessed of a true heart,
for he does not bear that belly which is difficult to fill and the cause of all meanness.
With one hand lifting her tresses of powdered hair and with the other raising her chin,
I beheld her face at the city gate, its ears washed by tears.
Though it is flickering and constantly causing her distress, that poor woman carries within her the sole root of her life, just as a nose carries the breath.
One part of my mind says, "I am going," while another part of my heart says, "I am not going.
O beautiful one, it is fitting for you to have two hearts, since your lover's heart has been stolen away.
Reclining on a bed of castor leaves, her heavy hips causing perspiration,
the peasant’s wife— like a bag of dust when she moves— dispels the fever of love.
Thus ends the section on the letter *e*, accompanied by the commentary *Vibhāvārthā*. The section on the letter *ka*:
"He leads my newly-wed bride, like a friend, to the place of dalliance; yet he does not approach me himself."
While the noble lady was thus praising her wife, the neighbor laughed.
"This is a *ketakī* flower, lovely in its seasonal progression"—such is the vain hope.
Just as its growth increases, so too does the profusion of its thorns.
O you who feign sleep and lend your ear to the sound of my sighs,
why do you pierce me with such sharp sighs, as if Love were a marksman who strikes by sound?
Where is that silk garment made of sloughed-off skin, and where is this series of serpent-jewels for adornment?
O Yamunā, by following in the path of the serpent Kāliya, you have become accessible to the whole world.
Not a single word was spoken by the fool, nor was a glance cast with favor;
when I fell at her feet, she did nothing but turn her parrot’s cage away.
As she gazes with eyes tremulous with passion, watched by young men who laugh, clap their hands, and stare at her,
the bee— though repeatedly driven away— dances upon her limbs as it falls back again and again.
The lotus-faced woman adorns the riverbanks by warding off [the flow] from all directions;
for the rivers, whose natural currents were unobstructed, and the women, with their tremulous eyes, are both now held back.
O gambler, that woman, whose movements were once slowed by modesty, has been made a mere pretension by you;
now, despite many gifts, she does not come, like a chessman on the board.
Who possesses such praiseworthy birth that even at midnight in the month of Māgha,
this sound of her girdle— prolonged by the wintry breeze— proclaims her good fortune?
What is impossible for love? She who once trembled even at the mention of a serpent now sleeps with the serpent on Śiva’s arm as her pillow.
For one who has been robbed by courtesans through a love that is like counterfeit gold,
the distress of losing wealth is as nothing compared to the great public ridicule.
O you with teeth and lips as red as the parva-day [cane], why do you not adorn your own body? He will abandon you, even on festival days, like a stalk of sweet sugarcane.
Alas, O rash woman! That ascetic on the road was touched by you with but half a glance;
yet that poor Brahmin body of yours was not recognized even from your sacred thread.
Even when my afflictions are being stretched out and gathered together, this [meditation] brings me joy;
it is like a rain of water from the celestial river falling upon a fierce, cloudless sky.
I consider the binding of a dam to be most appropriate for waters originating from a well—
those which cannot be obtained even by a king who possesses no merit.
Having wandered and now resting, though difficult to reach during the night, you— pierced by the tips of my fingernails like the sun ground upon a lathe—
are thin, yet you steal the gaze of the world.
What can I do, though I am attached day and night, for I am by nature cool? Alas, like my own shadow, I cannot bring happiness to my beloved, just as I cannot to myself.
The head is made heavy by hair; death results from falling into a pool of nectar;
and if there is a burden on the chest due to carrying a beloved, this is indeed incurable.

O beautiful one, even the knot of your pride is desirable, for it bestows a certain harshness upon my naturally sweet passion, just as the core of sugarcane provides a touch of astringency to its sweetness.
Who gave Giriśa the idea to place a serpent in his matted locks,
by which he was deprived of the pulling of the hair from the hand of his beloved during the passion of love?
Disregarding the blows from her hands, feet, girdle, and necklace, the lover, having seized her hair with force,
kisses the beloved’s face, whose lips quiver and whose eyes are reddened.
Now let her abandon her agitation and experience whatever state of pleasure she may;
nevertheless, O beautiful one, it will be like a stream of water drunk after eating myrobalan.
O you whose moon-like face is marked by the stain of collyrium tilaka, and whose hair is wet with dripping drops of water— whom,
like cotton for the fire of fresh separation, must you bring back to life?
For even when beset by hardships, the great do not abandon the service of others;
even elephants, though subsisting on mere blades of grass, keep their trunks moist with the flow of ichor.
"Why do you laugh? Why do you run about? Why do you call out to people, children, in vain?
Now show how he was seized by the throat by this one while unharmed."
With eyes softened and sweetened by timidity, a sidelong glance, longing, shame, and anger,
she turns toward him— neither to join nor to leave— having found her pleasure in this very state.
Attracted by the fragrance within the heart of the *ketaka* flower, these bees have swiftly approached from afar and gather its pollen, like the horses of the chariot of Madana.
What crookedness, what virtues, and what luster do the crescent moons possess,
once they have entered within and been overcome by that particular beast?
Having exerted various efforts at churning for the sake of overcoming both gods and asuras,
Viṣṇu, the Lord, desired to bestow auspicious fortune and sovereignty through a self-choice marriage (svayaṃvara).

"Daughter, why do you sleep amidst the fresh clouds under the delusion that they are boulders? Experience instead the wanderings to foreign lands caused by the thundering and the flickering play of lightning."
Having offended an innocent girl by saying "your lover was struck by my foot," why do you seek to appease her?
Is such a kick from the foot so easily obtained that it is as good as a favor?
This unfailing gaze of yours has reached Karna, as has this spear given by Indra;
neither has it failed to achieve victory, nor has it fallen to no purpose anywhere.
O fair-faced one, why do you weary your female messengers with what is impossible for your sidelong glance?
Even Kāma, fearing infamy, does not aim an arrow there.
Who could have known the value of the moon staked by the Lord in the game of dice,
that the daughter of the Mountain set her lower lip as the counter-stake for its victory?
O fierce one, I certainly do not release you out of fear of the blow of your foot;
rather, the bee, enduring the lash of the wind-shaken young shoots, resorts to the creeper.
O beloved, when the bow of the God of Love is drawn by the knitting of your brows in anger,
restrain those falling drops of tear-water, soot-blackened like bees whose wings have been severed from a snapped bowstring.
Could even Kāma not pierce the hearts of young women?
For their chests appear as if swollen from being struck by the arrows of a fool.
Why do you play with the lives of others, O lady with eyes sweet with wonder? Go far away, my friend;
let the snake-catcher play with the serpent in the courtyard without hindrance.
The connoisseur of aesthetic flavor strikes her limbs with his hands and feet as her eyes tremble with anger;
the more she provokes him with harsh words, the more he delights in his beloved.
Who censures her, and what fool would erase the pigment from the fruit of the God of Love? Who treats her as a thorn among jewels, and in whom does a lack of relish for the nectar arise?
While you wandered about with an angry hand playfully flicking a mango sprout,
that slender-bodied woman fainted, as if struck by the sword brandished in your hand like the God of Love.

"Enough of this noble lineage; let me enjoy her," so says Love. But when I consider that she is a *nakula* (mongoose), it is unavoidable that I, while enjoying her, will commit a slip of the tongue regarding my own lineage (*gotra-skhalana*).
Why, young fawn, do you abandon the rice-ear in this field?
This is merely a man of straw, with grass for arrows, grass for a bow, and fashioned from grass—a deceptive figure.
Thus ends the Section on the Letter *Ka*, accompanied by the commentary *Vibhāvya*.
The Section on the Letter *Kha*:
Friendship with the wicked is sweet at first, in the middle it is like the heat of summer, and at the end...
The friendship of virtuous people is delightful through its beginning, middle, and end.
Thus ends the section on the letter *kha*, accompanied by its commentary.
The section on the letter *ga*:
A wealthy man does not preserve the virtue he has acquired for long, whereas a poor man protects it.
O friend, a jar full of water sinks the rope in the water, but one that is empty does not.
Even a light person, when introduced by a guru, does not sink into the heart of the great,
just as a mountain brought by a boatman does not sink into the ocean.
The potent poison that went to the throat of the Lord of Gaurī was digested there;
however, malicious gossip does not digest when it reaches the ears of the great—it does not enter even slightly.
In front of the householder, the young woman— having described her lover’s state of love through deceptive words—
both pleases and torments him as she sighs again and again.
The elephant, who has surpassed excellent young women with his gait, should make his temples soiled with rut;
O small-bellied one, you who are a mere elephant in name—why do you carry pride?
Hearing her husband’s reproach for the offense of mispronouncing her family name,
the young woman casts a loving yet proud glance at her beloved and toward her friends.
Perceive, at the base of this pleasure grove fashioned during this season of summer,
coolness as if coiled up in the guise of the circular basin for irrigation.
"O friend, do not release this playful bird thinking its feet are bound by a string;
O simple one, on this branch with its coiled boughs, the restraint of the string will snap in an instant."

Before those whose ears and eyes are sealed by the fear of the teacher’s thundering voice and thick lightning, the young girl kisses her lover; for the arrow of passion is indeed more formidable than a thunderbolt.
Among the virtues of a housewife, humility, service, and obedience are counted as her qualities; for women with lovely eyes, pride, authority, and perversity are their ornaments.
Lakṣmī and Gaṅgā know the inner qualities or lack thereof in Hari and Hara:
one rejoices even at his feet, while the other does not dwell upon him even when placed upon his head.
Having undergone the risk of death, we have finally mastered the endurance of long separation;
yet you, merciless one, wish once again to impose upon us the difficult practice of sexual union.
Even when questioned about her lineage, she gave an answer exceedingly cool with virtue;
then, sighing, she cast her gaze upon her own body, which was now in vain.

O bee, you who grasp fragrances, whose every limb is now saturated with the exudation of blossoming *śāla* trees, and who have just now abandoned hundreds of trees after enjoying them— you no longer wander about.
When meeting those who are superior, you bow with your head; toward those who are inferior, you are uplifted; and toward equals, you remain level.
O Balance, you who know what is appropriate, why do you weigh gold against *guñjā* seeds?
As my wife is being led away, obstructed by my newlywed bride standing before me,
my heart splits in two, as if its very qualities were distributed between two boats.
Like a bow, even a single quality is sufficient for the attainment of the target if it is capable of drawing;
what is the use of many qualities that cannot withstand pressure, like the threads of a spider's web?
She sings songs, plays the flute, and strikes the lutes;
she causes the parrot in its cage to recite the syllables of your message, O beautiful woman.
This bee drinks the nectar incessantly without counting its expenditure;
yet the moon, possessing pride in his own good fortune, feels extreme envy toward the sun.
"O friend, you remain with your body still held together by its qualities; however, your heart has been carried away by him, just as fragrance is taken from a garland by the wind."
When I had come near to the teacher’s house and stood at his feet,
did my beloved not say something dear to me— even though she remained silent— by removing her anklet from her feet?
What is the use of knottiness for sugarcane? What is gained by the corruption of a song? What is the use of crookedness for the moon? And what is the use of poverty for a lover?
Even though my wife’s eyes were closed with a soft sigh at the moment of grasping my hair, she placed her foot upon my head upon seeing the thrill of horripilation on the cheek of her young daughter.
This eye, with its heavy lashes, its pupil rolling reddened by wakefulness, turns with great difficulty;
its brow is curved in anger caused by the placement of visible nail-marks.
Thus ends the section on the letter *ga*, accompanied by the commentary *Vibhāvya*.
The section on the letter *gha*:
[She is] one whose hips are joined, whose plump thighs are pressed together, and upon whom the entire weight of her breasts is cast.
Even while embracing her, the young girl says, "Let go! Let go!"
The lotuses, having closed their palāśa-like petals night after night, indeed sleep in peace;
but O night-lily, how can prosperity be guarded through constant wakefulness?
The lamp-flames flicker as they are deprived of oil,
and the hearts of the wives of travelers departing at dawn break like lotuses.
Thus ends the section on the letter *gha*, accompanied by its commentary. Now begins the section on the letter *ca*:
Having beheld the head of her fickle lover, his hair marked by the first streaks of grey, [she...]
Even at a time when weariness was appropriate, his wife took only delight.
O fierce one, even by touching you, who are so prone to anger, with my outstretched arm,
I am satisfied as if drinking from a muddy river through the stalk of a lotus.
O cool-scented breeze, who wander at night having been enjoyed and then discarded by fickle female serpents: O arrival of the dawn, go now to fulfill the hope of others.

Now the gaze of the deer-eyed woman, entangled by the moss-like rows of her long, curling locks that meet at the ends like those of a traveler on a long journey, is like a hand-poured stream of water, ever-flowing with tears.
O fierce one, because you are so fond of gazing at my thighs revealed by your trembling garment,
I did not even turn my eyes away from your feet for fear of the dust.

With her earrings swaying, her curls trembling, her garment slipping from her breasts, and her pair of thighs coming into contact [with each other], her eyes narrowed by the fatigue of the weight of her hips— this gait of hers captivates the heart.
O bee, you vainly scratch with your feet this sandy bed of pollen from the *ketakī* flower;
here dwells the very essence of beauty, a sea of honey that does not even have water within it.

O simpleton, you who have traveled for a long time with eyes rippling with suspicion, what do you look at? This is merely the line of scar-tissue from the wound caused by the embrace of your sword upon her.
Just as one blinded by intoxication strikes his own shadowy reflection with his trunk,
so too does this elephant, blocked before him, strike out at the opposing elephant.
Remembering her pair of thighs— which serve as the tethering pillar for the elephant of my heart, and from which saffron was stolen by her lower lip greedy for a kiss— I am not satiated.
Though she has turned her face away, this young woman— her neck bent sideways as she spreads out her hair— glances at you while creating a space for your gaze among her locks with her fingers.
Why do you cast your eye at dawn— its collyrium washed away by a kiss, its passion made manifest by sleeplessness— as if it were a half-moon arrow of the god of love, distressed by separation?
Thus ends the section on the letter *ca*, accompanied by its analytical commentary. Now begins the section on the letter *cha*:
The moon, which captures the reflection [of the sun], constantly assumes the state of being a deceptive counterfeit (*kūṭa*) of the lotus.
Having abandoned both [the gods and the asuras], the world praises only your face in the assembly.
Even while looking down at her mere shadow, Kṛṣṇa— with his head bowed and with rising fortitude—
pierces my heart, as skillfully as Arjuna strikes the wheel of Rādhā.
Thus ends the Section on the Letter *Cha*, accompanied by the commentary *Vibhāvya*.
**The Section on the Letter *Ja*** A few drops of water fell from your eye as you were making the effort to depart.
"Beloved, the ground I must travel over has been made slippery by these very things."
I remember her face, with its languid gaze, its collyrium blurred by drops of water, and its cheeks pressed by earrings constrained by her pair of arms stretched wide in a yawn.
Having awakened the Supreme Person in the forest, you carry him away in every direction;
this conduct of yours is most worthy of one as noble-born as you, and it is truly befitting the autumn season.
Thus ends the section on the letter *ja*, accompanied by its detailed commentary. Now begins the section on the letter *jha*:
By the clinking of bracelets as hands are tossed about, by leaning against pillars, and by silences—
O beautiful one, you adorn the door of the palace even with your parched weeping.
Thus ends the section on the letter *jha*, accompanied by the commentary *Vibhāvī*.
**The Section on the Letter *ḍha*** Like elephants, men beat the *ḍhakka* drum and display their intoxication for a long time.
Furthermore, the passion of women is like that of female elephants; it leads to the destruction of their own lineage.
Thus ends the section on the letter *ḍha*, accompanied by its commentary. Now begins the section on the letter *ta*:
"Alas, O fortunate one! While those arrows of Love torment her, they bring you joy."
The sun's rays heat the sun-stone, and they sweeten the moon.
O fair-limbed one, by the gain of you— who possess hips colored with many minerals like the slopes of Sānumatī—
I reach the heavens with a mere span of two fingers, as if gaining the ground of the best of mountains.
Having abandoned [the world], he relinquishes life; even when offered favor, he casts off all longing.
What more can be done for him by me than what the rainy season does for a lotus pond?
O fortunate one, in the calamity of separation from you, that slender-limbed woman— pale and possessing only her shadow—
is to be recognized like a female swan in the moonlight.
O fortunate one, she whose mind is fixed upon you has departed with her body alone,
like a river whose fish are trapped by a dense net, remaining now as nothing more than water.
Her heart, exceedingly hard yet agitated by the god of the uneven arrows, has burst open while clinging to you,
like the hem of a garment fluttering in the wind when it comes into contact with thorns.
O friend Chāyā, you who cannot bear to look upon the sun, you wander not even a single step without your covering; what can be done here? For embodied beings do not leave you behind.
In your absence, with the night prolonged and her aversion to the moon and sandalwood produced,
she was consumed like a lotus-stalk in the month of Māgha without fire.
O young woman, alas, your co-wife— though distressed by grief— does not drink from the cluster of blossoming *kaṅkelli* buds caused by the blow of your foot, for her conduct is crooked.

On the bed she was like a mistress; in the labor of love’s art, like a teacher; in her fatigue, like a servant; in the house, like the goddess Śrī; and before her elders, she was like modesty incarnate.
As long as you remain unattainable for me— who am unable to let you go even as I move toward you— you cannot be warded off by a wall, slipping away like a shadow.
This one, whose strength was matured by the hardships of asceticism, certainly did not exist even in Phālguna;
who now can endure Madana, intoxicated by spring, like the scorching sun?
O fortunate one, even the wall of her house has become pale, marked as if by the lines of the fingernails that counted the days of your departure.
O friend, I have been pierced by the glance of that rustic youth— glance which is crooked, affectionate, and sweet— and I am led solely by him, just as the earth is held by the tusk of a boar.
O banyan tree of the wretched village, let Vaiśravaṇa or Lakṣmī dwell in you;
yet your protection shall come from the very head of a buffalo at the blow of a commoner’s axe.
O lecher, enduring the fault of your noisy mouth and unable to abandon you, that slender-limbed woman carries you within her like a woodworm inside a carved statue.
O deer, these Śabara hunters will surely not spare you, who are like a mouthful of grass;
therefore, give up this life for the sake of fame alone, having engaged in battle with your horns raised.

O proud lady, just as Gaṅgā was the life-restorer for the enemy of Tripura when his head was offered after he had been consumed by the fire of love, so do you grant me life merely by grasping my hair.

O fortunate one, that lover has surely been made successful by you in secret among his friends, for he becomes talkative during conversations about you, appearing as if filled with reproach, joy, and feigned indifference.
O handsome one, as you walk along the path, her gaze, emerging from a gap in the hedge,
flashes like a minnow darting through a net of moss, trembling with fear.
O slender-limbed one, those who declare the conch shell to be heartless are themselves heartless, for it is that very shell which,
having accepted the leaf-like hand, performs the grasping of your hand.
Where now are those merchants, O Śakra-dhvaja, by whom your height was once established?
Those of the present day will desire to fashion you only as a wagon-pole or a sacrificial post.

Having reached a state of decline, love that is intensely concentrated through passion and desire instilled by another no longer shines, like the ear-ornament of amorous women when it has been severed.
When a man has lost his moisture and his vigor, like a piece of ginger that is withered and devoid of its essence,
even if he possesses wealth, the title "noble" (nāgara) is merely a mockery for one who is soiled.
In dense darkness, on a treacherous path, we have encountered a jackal with a torch in its mouth;
what shall we do, my friend, for even he stands there with his muzzle firmly closed?
O proud woman, for me who desires you, even my weighty virtues have turned into faults;
it is just like the ocean for one wishing to cross a river with muddy banks.
May this row of conch-shell bracelets— visible from afar even in the darkness, jingling loudly during a firm embrace in private— shatter along with the head of the householder.

O beautiful one, because of your conduct and your virtues, the hero— who had previously rolled about on your neck as if it were a pearl necklace perfectly suited to it— has now been made fickle again, like a string of pearls.
Thus ends the section on the letter *ta*, accompanied by the commentary *Vibhāvya*. Now begins the section on the letter *da*:
A housewife, her pride humbled by the sight [of her husband], her cheeks brimming with joy, [speaks].
Under the pretext of forbidding a kiss, she covers her face with both hands.
Stiffness of the body, stumbling, looseness, trembling, and meditation on the beloved;
at every step, an embrace of the sky—O passionate woman, what merit do you have for your secret tryst?
By the intense heat of separation from you,
her life has been shortened as days are lengthened, like a lotus plant by the summer season.
Even through association with the wicked, a virtuous person does not abandon their excellence of character;
the moon, though dwelling on the sun during every lunar phase, remains cool as soon as it emerges.
O fair-limbed one, as you walk in the darkness holding by the hand the messenger sent by your beloved,
you are visible from afar with the musk [on your forehead] washed away by your perspiration.
The virtues of your beloved have been brought to light by the very fault of your own mouth;
why do you grieve for the daily tearing down of the garden fence?
Do not despise this Sun because he displays gentleness out of courtesy;
for when he has assumed his fierce form, who can even bear to look upon him?
By her very glance, cast upon the face of her beloved with pupils trembling in the fear of separation,
the life-breaths of the deer-loving woman depart, as if afflicted by the arrows of a Pulinda hunter.
With hearts kept at a distance, their secrets hidden, and filled with excessive suspicion,
the embrace of the foolish is in fact a separation.
The elders are at the door, the parrot is in the corner, the child is nearby in the house, and my friends are here;
O beloved, forgive me for my inability to wait for the time, be gracious, for the festival day has arrived.

The beloved cowherd girl embraces her lover, who is charming as he presses his high breasts against her— breasts adorned with pearl-like drops of curd— as her own limbs grow languid from the exhaustion of churning.
O friend, by my beloved— who, with his teeth biting in agitation, aroused passion and deluded me— I have been led to the bed as if by betel-leaf.
Having made her beloved the object of her gaze—though he was mostly out of sight—she revealed her daughter;
then, with her heart struck by her own hand, she feigned embarrassment.
O fair-limbed one, as your eye rolls, displaying the rising of the Yamunā and possessing the playfulness of a brow,
it is as if the entire city has been conquered by you, O wielder of the plow, who casts down his plow.

The *bakula* tree, tender from being sprinkled with the essence of the wine-like breath of its beloved—so difficult to obtain when requested—causes pain in separation; where indeed is the familiarity of those who are naturally hard?
"O friend, why do you find comfort in his words, 'I shall return in two or three days,' when that nail-mark of yours,
deeply embedded, proclaims him to be a traveler on a long journey?"
O friend, why do you find fault with her hair, which has caused your feet to slip in the water of dharma awakened by the touch of your beloved, and which has made you chatter with a weight of pride?
Of what use is that wicked son born to a householder,
by whom his own family is turned to charcoal, like the planet Mars?

Those who display the loftiness of their bows, who are radiant with splendor, born of noble lineage, and as steadfast as diamonds even in the midst of waters— even in times of calamity, such heroes do not sink low.
O charming one, this gaze of yours strikes my life-breaths as they depart through the artistry of Love— even though he is fast asleep— just like an arrow from Arjuna’s mechanical bow.
The wife of a man in distress is moist with compassion for her son and filled with passion for her beloved;
being infatuated, she neither perceives nor rejects his advances for sexual union.
Like a destitute housewife sleeping in a dilapidated cottage, you pay homage to the moon;
we, however, with eyes deceived by the moonlight, sport upon our swinging cradles veiled in mist.
The wick of a lamp and a young woman of noble family attain a state of sootiness through their very cleverness;
even faults serve as ornaments for a courtesan and for the crescent moon.
The crimson rays of the sun, falling through the openings of the long windows,
enter the surface of the palace like the claws of the Man-Lion entering the chest of the Dānava.
With your eyes trembling slightly, your chest rising slightly, and your face smiling slightly—
let alone a flower, even the heroic Smara now finds it difficult with his painted bow.
This moon-faced woman, accompanied by her wicked friend, will not bring you happiness now;
like the full moon joined with the Viṣṭi day, may she not be pleasing to you during the night.
While the householder is angry and driving the bull away from the heap of threshed straw,
the farmer’s wife and her brother-in-law laugh, their faces watching him closely and secretly.
Those jewels and heroic men who were fashioned for the sake of brilliance may indeed shine;
yet their splendor leads only to their own destruction, like that of fragile blades of grass.
Thus ends the section on the letter *da*, accompanied by the commentary *Vibhāvārthā*.
**The Section on the Letter *dha*** O Fire, cause tears to fall with your smoke; burn [him] with your flame, which is soiled by burning; burn him with your embers!
Even on this wintry night, the impoverished housewife will wake you.
"Maintain your composure; let the night pass, O fair-faced one, and let him too remain full of longing.
Enter deeply into his heart like an arrow of Love, released for a moment."
At the city gate, I shall behold her body— marked by white nails, with its ornaments cast aside, its eyes hidden by disheveled locks, and its tears doubled by my gaze.
Even when undertaking a righteous deed, for the wicked, the sole motive is the injury of others;
rain experiences no cause in the consecration of crows.
Thus ends the Section on the Letter *Dha*, accompanied by the commentary *Vibhāvya*. Now begins the Section on the Letter *Na*:
In the cool season, amidst the swelling sands rugged with the descent of rivers...
The rivers shine with their banks that appear like thick layers of cotton-wool.
Resting in the shadow of her own body to dispel the affliction of the summer heat, alas,
this charming female deer performs various graceful movements of her limbs.
O friend, even though he is old, Nanda does not laugh when the cowherd women bow before him;
for that son of Yaśodā is one in whom the god of love eternally blossoms.
Even when her body has been offered and brought to its natural state, a loving woman does not abandon her wilfulness;
Pārvatī, who is interwoven with half of Hara’s body, is the illustration of this.
Trembling with pride in the beauty of his own wife, which he infers from the enjoyments of city-dwellers,
the weaver does not set foot upon the ground in the presence of his kinsmen.
O friend, who is that man who enters at night and casts his gaze upon the corner of her foot? Indeed, he is a villain who, before the world, proclaims his own greatness.
If even a great man, once released, were somehow unable to be restrained,
would he not surely turn back upon his liberator like the poison of Mount Mandara when it was churned up?

Who that has other means of passage would resort to a bridge of wood that is to be traversed with fixed steps, which brings disaster if one stumbles, and which is moreover presided over by a wicked ruler?
For both elephants who delight the world with the quality of their own gait and for true poets,
it is only virtuous people who add to their splendor, even as they carry great majesty.
It does not lose its luster when heated, it does not melt, it does not go out, nor does it become soiled;
his love shines night after night like a jewel-lamp.
My love for kings, even though they have been repeatedly bestowed upon me, surely abandons them;
it remains fixed right there, like a potter’s wheel that continues to spin after being turned.

Even though I have gazed upon her full and well-enjoyed hips in the morning, drinking them in with my eyes, I am not yet satiated, like a ruddy goose gazing at the orb of the cool-rayed moon against a sky without clouds.
I remember that fair-limbed woman, her thighs pressed closely together, fanning herself with her hand placed upon breasts heaving with sighs, her eyes tender yet angry, exhausted by love-making.
Know that "devoid of qualities" and "dead" are two terms expressing the same meaning;
behold, they describe this [bow] here as being devoid of its string and lifeless.
O youth, may this monkey hanging from your own fine thread-like [hair] steal your gaze for a moment;
he stands before you like a crab that has seized a hook.
This fair-limbed woman is adorned by her very presence in the village, like a city song;
musk does not acquire a foul odor merely from dwelling within the belly of a deer.
O you whose breasts are marked by nail-scratches, whose back is covered with peacock feathers, and whose limbs are languid as they toss upon the ground—
you steal my heart like a flower-arrowed god who has emerged from the rending of your chest.
She has been reduced to insignificance, yet you bestow upon her excessive weight;
like a burden borne by one unaccustomed to heavy loads, domestic life becomes exceedingly difficult to carry.
Neither a female messenger, nor entreaties, nor folded hands, nor the casting of side-long glances—
O friend, for those who pride themselves on their own desirability, the seizing of the hair is the first act of seduction.

At night, for the couple who have been impelled by the arrows of the flower-bowed god and who have found the essence of pleasure in silence, the mind continues to sport in that very same way, its knot never loosened.
Having extracted all the essence, even though it was placed within her own body as if inseparable from it,
the female serpent casts off its slough, and the courtesan abandons the man.
O fair-limbed one, you release with great difficulty your bodice, which is damp with the sweat of dancing fatigue,
like a creeper on Madana’s bow shedding its garment moistened by the water of nectar.
O fair-limbed one, I do not say that you are ill-behaved or of fierce conduct;
rather, a fear easily arising from the very nature of love wells up within my heart.
Surely you were not scrutinized by my friend with more than a mere third of a glance,
since she offers a flower as if to her own neck when you have turned away.
Proclaiming their offenses against their beloved through merciless bites with the nails and teeth, blows with the fists, and passionate embraces, the impassioned women effect a reconciliation.
O daughter of Surabhi, no regard was paid to your qualities, nor to your marks, nor to your age, nor to your form;
this bell has been fastened upon you simply because you are the daughter of Kapila.
Victory to the married couple, whose offenses are causeless, whose quarrels, anger, and joys are causeless,
and for whom life, death, pleasure, and pain are shared in common.

You cannot be grasped by my two hands, yet you do not depart from my heart; you cause me torment like the splinter of an arrowhead from the flower-weaponed god that remains lodged within me after being broken.
Where "Lord" is the appropriate harsh term, "Beloved" is the insult, and "Slave" is the mark of favor—that alone is true matrimony; otherwise, the woman is a rope and the man is a beast.
Even though she has been laid to rest, that same beloved alone flashes in my mind,
like a row of letters on a leaf appearing through the superimposition of another line.
O slender-waisted one, this line of hair upon the slope of your hips is like a creeper placed there as a marker for the location of a hidden treasure; it entices you.
O fortunate one, you take away the heart of that woman whose eyes are half-closed;
it is not fitting for you to swallow her arm while merely offering your finger.
Having been led to the inner chamber and having been granted a single night’s vigil with great respect,
by which youths were you not released in no time, like a leaf from the tree of Durgā?
Whatever splendor exists in the stars, in fire, in the moon, in the belly [of Agni], in gold, in jewels, in the eye, and in the ocean—
all that is indeed the radiant power of the friend of the lotus (the sun).
She possesses neither her own caste, nor her beauty, nor any refinement, nor even her original nature;
in the calamity of separation from you, the young girl has become like a language fallen into corruption.

You have no concern for ornaments; you conquer young men by the excellence of your very form, O friend, like the science of wrestling which, having set aside arrows and weapons, triumphs over the flower-arrowed god of love.
O friend, just as my beloved, drawn by my eyes, whirls around again and again exactly as he is, so does he churn my heart like a churning-stick churns a vessel of curd.
Fashioning various beautiful forms of diverse colors, that slender woman,
like an artist’s brush, paints you upon every wall.
Thus ends the section on the letter *na*, accompanied by its analytical commentary. Now begins the section on the letter *pa*:
A cowherd girl, attached to a traveler and unguarded, perceived nothing of the deep rumbling of the clouds.
O row of parrots, you flee in vain at the *huṃ* sounds of our playful arts.

The woman separated from her beloved bows down to, gazes at, kisses, and embraces her left vine-like arm— which throbbs with the anticipation of union with her lover— with her limbs budding with horripilation.
You have entered but do not know how to exit;
you experience agitation like Abhimanyu within that woman’s heart, which is like a *cakravyūha* formation.
Behold how the crow on the mango blossom is rendered vocal by the bee;
moreover, the swarm of bats gathers in agitation around the bud of the cotton plant.
O fair-faced one, why do you wish to grasp from the hand of my friend the mirror whose surface is filled with reflections, in vain through the delusion that it is a play-lotus?
O friend, I see you like the moon that, having descended from the peak of the eastern mountain, now dwells in the midst of the sky, with your pride diminished like a shadow.
Even from the corner of the courtyard, that lord of the night, composed of nectar, removes my fever;
yet, O friend, he does not do so if the master of the house restrains me like a nocturnal fever.
O fortunate one, she whose limbs are withered by the bristling of her hair at the mere sight of her own reflection, and who is filled with fear even at her own shadow,
now hastens toward you in the darkness, tearing through the thorns.
The parrot is the guarantor against the opposing side; the conversation of love is the wager with the elders;
the role-reversal is the stake with that young girl—let the prize be considered accordingly.
O pitiless young woman, this side-glance of yours, released for the sake of supreme enchantment, enters the heart like an arrow drawn to the ear; it does not emerge.
With her toes touching the ground, her eyes sweet with both joy and fear,
the slender-limbed girl did not fall because she pressed her chin against the top of the wall.
O friend, there is no shame in this man who comes in the morning and speaks falsehoods;
for he feels no embarrassment even at the burnt blackness that clings to his face.
Behold, O slender-waisted one, how the sun, having approached Phālguna and conquered his adversaries,
brings back the cattle like the son of Virāṭa.
In this world, the coolness cast out by the summer heat takes refuge in these three difficult places: the forest of negligence, the mountain of your breasts, and the roots of deep lakes.
O fortunate one, this night, long with wakefulness, wipes away your transgression, crushes your pride, and robs you of your peace; it strikes down the oaths you yourself have sworn.
When the beloved arrived from afar, their first reunion was as if it were unprecedented; yet pride, weeping, and conciliation occurred again at the beginning of the imminent sexual union.
Upon the peak of the eastern mountain, this darkness— pierced by the rays of the approaching sun and drenched in blood—
shines like the body of Andhaka impaled upon a trident.
With her navel turned upward, the three folds of skin effaced, the tips of her breasts darkened, and her eyes languid,
her body— with its many white lines upon her hips— cannot endure the act of a man.
O lady of delicate limbs, why do you carry this sweat-water when your amorous play has only just begun?
You are like the vine of the flower-arrowed god’s bow, bent down to fix the string, dripping with honey.
O beautiful one, show your moon-like face to men, dispelling even their slight thirst;
let the public rumor established that "he is conquered by his wife" become my fame.
Let the autumnal night spread forth, and let the light of the cool-rayed moon whiten the worlds;
yet even this is no more than a mere trifle to the female cakora birds within their cages.
"Anxious because you have been traveling for a long time, O traveler who has arrived first, the trees along the path,
their branches flushed with color, will explain your delay when you reach them."

The mind remembers her as her garment fell away, her hands placed upon her breasts, her thighs covered by her firm hips, and the lamp shaken by hundreds of "phūtkṛti" breaths from her lips bitten by his teeth.
Upon the mountain, where clusters of great medicinal herbs and jewels flash all around like a pleasure-couch,
the serpent glides with a single gem fixed upon him, appearing like a fallen girdle-string.
In the rainy season, you wander through the quarters of the sky, covering the slopes of the mountain ranges;
O cloud, you who are fickle at heart, what can be said of you? You are subject to the wind.
