This hem of your garment, its fringe worn away day by day and pulled down too far,
speaks of your own extremely wretched husband, like a desolate village.
O traveler, how do you endure this unbearable, flickering, and brilliant [heat], which pours forth drops of water from the clouds—
like molten gold from the city of Maya, yet tempered by the fire of Śiva’s arrow?
O young woman, with your delicate tremor and your most sweet luster, you bring comfort to the traveler sleeping from fatigue—
your braid hanging down like a branch laden with fruit.
She, whose hips and thighs are full and lofty, does not grant entrance even to others;
for you have become like a driven-in wedge in her heart, invisible from the outside.
Just as her son-in-law sleeps in the morning with limbs disheveled and exhausted,
so too does his mother-in-law, her mind filled with joy, regard him with increasing respect.
Though moved by affection, my beloved was made to stiffen by me with side-long glances of feigned anger; trembling with fear, he was then seized around the neck with a sudden burst of laughter.
O heart, if you are rent asunder by the cruel conduct of your beloved, even that rending is praiseworthy,
like the hem of the garment spread out as a couch for the battlefield of their amorous play.
The bee, greedy for the lotuses in the distant expanse of water due to the fragrance brought by the wind,
fails to examine his own position and, alas, meets with calamity.
With her jar-like breasts bristling with great horripilation as they are dwarfed by the chest of Keśava out of love, the charming young bride silently mocks the weightiness of Mount Govardhana.
Unable to endure separation from their beloveds, even the co-wives— who are by nature their enemies—
protect the lives of these fawn-eyed women, fearing the ruin of their own households.
O messenger, you manifest an excessive passion that brings a certain crookedness to this speech, yet it delights my beloved at every step, like the song of a parrot.
For the young girl entering the heart of her beloved, which is already occupied by powerful women,
the path is cleared by the sword of her eyes, rippling with fresh, sharp, and piercing glances.
Is one whose love is firmly rooted carried away by mere childish curiosity, when there are already the expertise in dalliance, trust, favor, anger at the offense of a lover's request, and so forth?
Your venerability arises solely from your past deeds, even though you are now aged;
O elephant, abandon this pride, for by its very scent you are to be trumpeted at by young men.
She who was somehow first led into the bedchamber by her friends does not, as it were, hear the signal for departure in the morning.
Without worship there is no consecration, and without mantra there is no consecration;
let one who errs regarding both of these look upon the stone of Indra.
In the housewife, there is a greater degree of respect, love, and trust, along with an even greater sense of fear;
this speaks of a passion that is as undivided as that of a young girl.
Familiar with the sensation of embracing the jar-like breasts, firm and full, of Pulikata,
Śiva’s serpent used as a sacred thread longs for the goddess’s display of jealous pride.
The joy that arose in the housewife at the thought, "My beloved has arrived from afar,"—
that too became a hundred-peaked mountain out of pride because he had arrived before her guests.
"Give me your back; do not touch me; move far away, you who have turned your face away!
Even so, the boatman pursues you, for this boat is drawn along by the ropes of your virtues."
The garment sent by my beloved, marked by the joining of her two hands stained with saffron,
instructs me to perform thousands of salutations with joined palms.
Screened by a wall, she offers her lip to the face of her beloved,
just as the night, veiled by the eastern mountain, offers the glow of twilight to the day.

O rogue, you who have been drained by unchaste women who are merciless toward their husbands, do not take me away in anger; scorched by the burning of my possessiveness, I weep as I behold your emaciation.
When, in the very courtyard, embracing me with her jar-like breasts trembling from emotion,
she rests her face upon my shoulder and bathes my back with her tears.

The young woman kisses the face of the dead man— his face watched by ghosts with flickering flames from their mouths— while he is gazed upon by dogs shedding tears and by spirits who stumble over their morsels of food.
Indeed, a slanderer should be conquered by placing another slanderer before virtuous people;
Viṣṇu conquered Bāṇa in battle by manifesting his own fever.
O honey-drinker, drink the bakula bud by placing just the tip of your tongue at a distance;
you are needlessly applying your mouth to the honey when it can be fully enjoyed as a mere smear upon your lower lip.
For generally, those who are themselves impure resort to the company of the impure; the breaking of the banks of the Yamunā results in the crushing of the coils of the serpent Kāliya.
Behold, O fortunate one, Umā, out of fear of being separated from her beloved body, remains joined to the body of the moon-crested Lord and carries the Ganges upon her head as her sole deity.
In regions that serve as the mother-source for the rivers of tears from the eyes of the wives of travelers,
the Creator has, as it were, encircled a circle of clouds with Indra’s bow.

Even though he had come from afar with great difficulty, the master of the house was hidden for one day by his wife, who was addicted to excessive dalliance, from her neighbors, friends, and relatives.

Like a dirty garment belonging to another, you have been mercilessly used by those women even after they have eaten; O base one, you have been released by these unchaste women without their taking anything from you.
Thus ends the Section on the Letter *Pa*, accompanied by the commentary *Vibhāvākhyā*.
**Section on the Letter *Ba*** When her hair was reddened with lac by many women, her lover was mocked by his friend.
The modesty felt at that moment betrays her good fortune among her friends.
The heart of her mass of hair, which has abandoned its state of being bound,
seems as if it were rent asunder under the guise of its parting marked with vermilion.
As the merchant, choked with heavy pride, declared, "Strength also dwells within me," his wife looked at the faces of the people with a concealed smile.
The bee, drawn by the fragrance of a freshly blossomed lotus wafted by a strong wind,
is pulled toward the lotus plant as if by a fishing line cast from its nose.
A virtuous person treats even a great fault as if it were no fault at all, just as Hari [Vishnu] treated the arrow;
however, malicious people remain awake regarding every fault, like thieves.
Although your disposition is momentary like that of a Buddhist, you are one who has many favorites;
yet, just as a broken eyebrow does not remain broken, your friendship never falters.
As the husband and wife, crying out "O mistress, turn back!
and "O beloved, go!", spent the day on the bank of the lake following him until the point of departure.
Reflecting in my mind upon those playful amorous gestures of my youth, which she was no longer capable of performing, I now grieve for that very wife who has been deprived of honor.
Thus ends the section on the letter *ba*, accompanied by the commentary *Vibhāvya*.
**The Section on the Letter *bha*** You wander about, you show your teeth, you stretch out your hand, and you take even a blade of grass as your refuge.
Fie on your pride, O elephant! You do not offer your life into the fire of your own belly.
Fire makes even a blade of grass consist of prosperity when it is attached to it;
I suspect that you too have attained this very state of gold because of the obstruction of your own greatness.
In this long summer, the night becomes slender like the Yamunā river here,
while the days, like islands, likewise become broader in their course.
O traveler, she— cast by you into the great fire of passion like a golden pill—
is so delicate that even with her hand, she cannot be touched by the impure.
With one earring swaying upon the ground and her bodice disarrayed, this charming girl,
as she gazes [at him], blows away even the cloud of passion with her sighs.
Embraced by a serpent-woman, you have indeed become a sovereign of serpents;
yet, desiring the breast of a forest-dwelling woman, your lightness of character manifests itself.

"You are victorious, O Protector! For, having been gazed upon by his wife with a favorable look, the village chief—who eats only alms—was praised thus: 'Since you alone are at ease in the empty assembly of the gods.'"
For an old servant who is incapable of enjoyment, who provides protection merely by his glance, and who does not even face [his master],
even a young woman or royal fortune serves only for his sustenance.
On that night when you shall be there to rest your feet and soothe the fatigue of the journey,
he will forcibly cast me upon his chest, my legs bound by his clasping arms.
O friend, for one who attains the state of being adorned— whether it be gold purified by rubbing or a man whose passion has been refined— the possession of weight (or excellence) is entirely fitting.
Since you possess a heart full of affection even for Giriśa, who is but a man of ashes, you are rightly fortunate;
thus, the popular rumor that you are the daughter of Oṣadhiprastha is proven false regarding you.
Awakened by passion, heaving sigh after sigh, he who was drenched with love gazes during her sleep upon the young woman’s thick thighs, which had been covered out of fear.
Like a female bee drawn by fragrance within the interior of a bud, following the flower,
she wanders in the darkness at that rendezvous, humming indistinctly.
Having cast aside her modesty, she remained here and there in your affection as if it were water, circling again and again like a boat caught in a whirlpool.

O daughter of a plowman, you who are full of virtues, you cause these young men— who are worthy of embracing your neck— to wander about near your own dwelling, like the tethering rope for a bull at the hitching post.

O Lord, though there is fire in Your forehead-eye, the moon upon Your crest, and the jewels of serpents as lamps upon Your body, You remain composed entirely of darkness; for who can transcend their innate nature?
Thus ends the Section on the Letter *Bha*, accompanied by the commentary *Vibhāvya*. Now begins the Section on the Letter *Ma*:
Just as the young girl, her shame dispelled by the intoxication of wine, speaks face-to-face—
The beloved drinks from her mouth in such a manner that he never reaches satiety.

Having consulted with his friends and made it his primary concern, he has even begun this slaughter; yet this pride of his is destroyed by the embarrassment on his face, just as the wealth of the virtuous is lost through the shame of their countenance.
O wise woman, that you give even your back to me, a passionate man, as I offer my hand,
I consider that too to be my own good fortune, like that of the friend of the lotus (the sun).
"Do not touch me! she said as if in anger, yet no shame was betrayed;
when embraced, she said with a smile, "O immodest one, what are you doing?"
O Godāvarī, intoxicated by the wine of the clouds, why do you tear asunder the roots of the *nicula* trees and the hearts of the unchaste women dwelling on your banks?

Just as the excellence of the qualities of sandalwood trees is for nothing but the disregard of those fallen into the company of the dull-witted, so too is the preeminence of the virtues of the steadfast.
O friend, why do you vainly compare yourself to Tulasī at the garland upon the head of the Slayer of Madhu?
For it is the manifestation of your own fragrance that serves to perfume her feet.
Having made a pact by counting the number of days until he would go to her, she was thus consoled by her beloved;
meanwhile, that night passed, incapable of sexual union.
The forest is the source of musk, and even the farmer’s garden bears saffron;
yet you alone, O courtesan of the marketplace, are the very essence of all the city's wealth.
O friend, just as a bee wandering among the days of spring enters the mind,
so too does the arrow of Love, which resembles a sharp iron thorn.
O beloved, when I move away, your glances naturally release their water;
truly, these priceless tears immediately attain the state of necklaces for my heart.
O innocent one, all five arrows of Love are constantly lodged in my mind;
I suspect that he has placed two pellets in the form of your breasts upon your heart.
Alas, the melodies following the hollows of the flute placed against the mouth of the Slayer of Madhu steal my heart, just like the reed-arrows of the God of Love.
O friend, the continuous union of two great, well-rounded, heart-captivating,
and exalted noble persons is like that of two breasts.
O friend, though I have been repeatedly restrained by many and have contemplated it myself again and again, delusion has arisen in that direction and does not turn back.
O best of trees, you have been carried away by the great waters of the Narmadā through the tossing of her wave-eyes;
if you are called "fallen," even such a fall is praiseworthy for you.
The trembling of Śiva’s hand during the marriage ceremony— delayed by his clasping of Mena’s hand— caused Menā to rejoice, made Hari smile, and turned Giri (the Mountain) away in shame.

When shall I, casting aside her face— which is fragrant as honey, with its tilaka-mark melting from the heat of passion, whose speech falters, and whose reddish eyes roll— drink the nectar of her lower lip?
Out of pride that you have many lovers, not even a footstep of yours falls upon the earth;
by which young men have you not been embraced and cast off like a shuttle from its garments?

Just like sugarcane, which is naturally sweet at its root but becomes tasteless toward the tip, other men— who offer sweetness at first but turn sour later— should be placed among various [other] types of people.
O friend, though he was placed in great affection, offered many flowers, and honored in many ways, my beloved remains perverse like the planet Saturn, O wicked graha!
O young Śabara woman, do not harbor pride on account of the weight of your full breasts,
which possess such beauty even when adorned with the sloughs cast off by female serpents.
O friend, why does he— embracing my shadow upon the ground while his hair stands on end with thrill— not make me free from anger, since he does not abandon his nature of affection?
Like one robbed in the moment of separation, like an enemy in the battle-game of the flower-arrowed god,
or like a servant at the time of toil— I am never satiated while embracing the lady of curved limbs.
Why do you release me from my resolve, O proud one, with such a surge of doubled indignation? For fire born of affection flares up with water, and anger is provoked by conciliation.
Setting aside the thick sandalwood paste and making the fanning with their arms an obstacle to its interruption,
the couple embraces, disregarding the summer heat due to the torment of love.
For those of noble mind place trust even in the great, while the base do not place even a little trust in the small;
the ocean conceals even mountains, but the rivers in summer do not conceal even a frog.

O proud one, though you are harsh, you do not relinquish your innate sweetness, just as a stream of honey does not lose its sweetness; even when you knit your brows, you grant me delight, like a river flowing into the ocean.
O housewife, by the sounds of the lute strings— like the strikes from bowstrings drawn by the god of love— whose heart among the young travelers does not tremble?
Her fear, her anger, and her despondency, as well as my own bashfulness,
arose in the midst of the sky as we both lowered our necks to conceal our smiles.
Let her run about naked, or let the river of three paths (the Ganges) suddenly fall;
this Narmadā alone possesses a flavor suited to my lineage.
O friend, at night, attend upon him who is anointed with musk and clad in blue garments,
like a beautiful female bee upon a blue lotus in the Yamunā.
Having come within the range of my friend’s vision, no one at all is able to move;
O traveler, you have fallen into the treacherous snare of the flower-bannered god’s bower-house.
O fortunate one, even that which is unpleasant, when fashioned out of great affection, becomes endurable;
indeed, the destruction of youth through the birth of a son does not lead to sorrow.
Out of the heavy anger caused by the seizure of my pride, it is only my beloved who is pleasing to me,
like a golden ornament that has become pure through the heat of fire.
Thus ends the Section on the Letter *Ma*, accompanied by the commentary *Vibhāvākhyā*. Now begins the Section on the Letter *Ya*:
She abandons the thorny branches that grasp at the hem of her garment as she passes by the youth.
Knowing you alone to be a man, she wanders even in the city as if in a forest.
"O wise ones, we have approached you merely through our proficiency in speech;
it was not realized that even among you there exists one who is devoid of devotion."

Where there was no female messenger, where even affectionate glances were not cast by the clever girl, and where words were not yet spoken— even now that emotion has been revealed through her passion.
O friend, I consider the life of that woman to be as dark as the Yamunā, who was led away by her co-wife after entering [the house] and being seized by a serpent.
In whom even infamy is fame, modesty is an obstacle, pride is indeed immorality, and being slighted is the recognition of virtue— O friend, have you not seen such a young man?
Whatever greatness is observed among the wicked through some stroke of fate is like the whiteness of crows; indeed, even that does not last long before leading to misfortune.
Indeed, that love which attains supreme purity even when cast into the fire of the foul-mouthed— such love, like a garment purified by fire, is rare to find in this world.
Because he does not seek a limit [to his giving] and bestows his entire fortune as provisions for the journey,
my mind has been filled with an exceedingly terrible apprehension.
O young woman, by your face, which possesses the beauty of a lotus and spreads the enmity of jealousy among the youths,
the entire village has been thrown into agitation, as if by a villain.
May this union of yours, which will endure for as long as life lasts, which possesses an identical disposition and is utterly inseparable like two rivers, bring forth even greater aesthetic flavor.
I remember her, heavy with pride and anger, as she struck me on the head with her foot, saying, "O rogue, let that very garland which you wear as a crest-jewel go back to you!"

A farmer’s wife, who maintains her youthfulness in secret from her husband, feigns innocence among her kinsmen, and displays straightforwardness toward her elders, is praised by young men under such pretexts.
O beautiful one, he who was never before restrained by his teachers, nor by friends, nor even by discernment, nor by the laughter of his enemies— he has been brought to a state of discipline by you.

O tree, whose roots are moistened by water, whose flowers bloom at every joint, and which is laden with fruit on all sides— you rejoice without considering that this is merely the transformation resulting from your acquaintance with the waves.
May he who bears upon his lap a friend sleeping with hands folded in exhaustion from the battle with Cupid carry the pride of his virtues like the silk garment of the bow-string of Love.
If elephants dwell even on the seven-leaved tree merely from the scent of its flowers,
why does the elephant bear his temples soiled with the mud of rut?
From the moment this daughter of the village chief grew up and became as radiant as a cluster of blossoming *śaṇa* flowers, she has been fond of yellow garments.
O flower-gatherer, a blue lotus trembling on the waves of the Yamunā is not easily obtained by you,
unless the humming bee, following its fragrance, wanders there.
Thus ends the Section on the Letter Ya, accompanied by the commentary Vibhāvya.
Now begins the Section on the Letter Ra: Of Kṛṣṇa, whose crown has been washed by the waters of royal consecration, [there is this] account in his stories...
With eyes languid from the weight of pride, Rādhā gazes upon her lotus feet.

That house becomes a different kind of dwelling where the master of the home rejoices at the pulling of his hair by the hand of his beloved, who is angry during a lovers' quarrel; otherwise, it is merely a front porch or a leaf-hut.
"Today I realize that the popular saying, 'The king is ill,' is true;
for you, O fortunate one, have come to the edge of my bed while still possessed of health."
As my beloved bowed before me, his natural flow of speech obstructed by his friends,
my passion surged toward him with double intensity, like a river rushing toward its downward slope.
"This is beauty, this is splendor, this is excellence, this is goldwork;
O graceful one, you wander from door to door at every mansion, meeting with the destitute."
The young bride disdainfully offers food— even if it is stale and made warm by her own sharp, bitter sighs— into the mendicant’s bowl fashioned from the leaves of a forest bower.
Indeed, she does not maintain her own independent status;
rather, like a string of pearls, she remains exactly as she is, made subservient by the virtues of that leader who establishes her.
O slender-limbed one, you shine like a vessel of auspiciousness with a mango sprout—
your face kissed by that very [sprout] which has manifested its first flush of passion.
A young woman who is led by one lacking in physical beauty and virtue becomes as light as dust tossed by the wind; yet, when led by one of great virtue, she spreads her own weightiness like the sun.
When fresh passion unfolds, with eyes slow and languid due to the gradual onset of separation,
this glance— smiling yet bashful— proclaims that the desired goal has been achieved.
Even the anger of passionate women is neither harsh nor long-lasting;
for even a stone from the rainy season is very smooth and lasts but a moment.
O friend, this weeping is blessed; what more need be said? Even death would be priceless to me, for it was ordained by him who steals the heart and eyes as if in a dream.
O friend, by my very anger— though he was crooked, knotted, and hard—
I have instantly brought him to straightness, like a bamboo cane with heat.
This mother of the Pitṛs first approached to usher in the night;
she herself colors the moon, just as a wicked messenger corrupts a bad leader.
Thus ends the section on the letter *ra*, accompanied by its commentary. The section on the letter *la*:
Alas, you have become attached to the path of darkness; O wick, though well-oiled, you are now consumed by fire.
Does this one, so dear to the eyes of all, perhaps touch again that which was once enjoyed and then abandoned?
Fortune teaches these virtues, whereas misfortune shakes them off;
for when full, the moon is well-rounded, but in its waning, it becomes crooked.
O friend, with its openings blocked by plucked threads, this empty dwelling where birds alight seems to weep as that traveler departs, its face covered by the hem of his garment.
Erotic passion adorns you, clinging to her broad hips— which sport like the trunks of elephants— just as a rutting elephant clings to a rampart.
Neither her face, nor her limbs, nor her wings, nor her feet were stained by pollen;
as if avoiding contact, the clever bee drank the honey from the lotus.
The nail-mark on her hip is fading, and my heart is withering;
this meal is indistinct and tasteless, yet it is full of passion and accompanied by distress.
To put the enemy of Madhu— who has drunk in the hearts of all the gopīs— to shame, Rādhā,
like one ignorant, asks about the story of Śambhu, who is satisfied with only half of his beloved.
On the shores of the Ocean of Milk, beautiful-eyed women sing the glories of Rādhā— she whose arms are the essence of the milk-ocean, solidified by the fire of Lakṣmī’s sighs.
When I stepped outside the pleasure-chamber as a guest at her feet among my friends, my beloved manifested her favor by placing a fan at the window.
Thus ends the section on the letter *la*, accompanied by the commentary *Vibhāvya*. The section on the letter *va*:
There is no removal of color upon the forehead, nor is there any trembling of the limbs, nor a bite upon the lip.
The lotus was taken away without even touching the water by one skilled in means.
Upon the chest of her beloved, made uneven by the swelling wounds of various weapons,
both Fortune and the Hero’s bride sleep soundly, their hair standing on end with pride.
O beloved, though turned away from me, your sighs— like arrows discharged by an unfair warrior— pierce my heart even as they fall upon my back.
O wine-eyed one, it is now evident that Khaṇḍa has arrived at your lips;
for, being greedy for the singular essence of fresh nectar, I did not see him anywhere else.
As the young couple fanned one another, all their limbs became separated;
yet their hips, as if bound by true friendship, did not part even in the midst of the intense summer heat.
The dawn twilight dispels the anger of the proud woman, the darkness of the sky, the buffalo from the field, and the bee clinging to the lotus.
As her chest expands, the bodice breaks apart at her breasts;
yet not even the slightest trace of affection for your former lover breaks within your heart.
Having observed another individual, it was understood that [the quality] resides in her alone;
but now I know you to be common to both, like the face of Indra upon the palace.
Like a fan moving back and forth near you who dispel the heat,
my friend’s mind has been made restless, as if it were the hem of your garment.
O slender-limbed one, you bestow flavor within me and extend your moist affection,
for like a river with water within, you dwell inside me even though you are invisible from without.
The proud man, whose various attachments have been established and who has been disregarded by his own arrogance,
how can he attain awakening— he who remains asleep even while awake?

Fearing that her beloved might turn away in shame or lose his affection, the young woman, sweetening her speech with a plaintive tone, casts a glance toward him— glance that is moist with love yet tinged with the guilt of her transgression.

O fair-limbed one, you who rest upon my chest, with heavy breaths, whose only armor is speech, and who are drenched in sweat— stay, for you have conquered me, O lady adorned with a forehead-mark placed upon your brow!
The god of the five arrows, his eyes unsteady with passion for Rādhā, roams all around Kṛṣṇa and discharges his shafts,
purified by piercing through the ten directions, at their vulnerable points.
When even the Lord, though possessing four faces, became averse and fell into a state of powerlessness regarding the rescue of the submerged earth,
Hari’s hair stood on end with supreme wonder.

O *ketaka* branch, your dwelling is by the edge of a pond, your fences are thorns, and the bees that visit you are ever wakeful; why then, with all these, do you not ward off the fragrance of your own blossoms?
O charming girl, though you are held fast, you tremble; thus you enter my heart, which delights in its own agitation, as if the power of the flower-bowed god were touching a target that is trembling.
O friend, your body, having engaged in an unequal battle with arrows and having surpassed the splendor of Gāṅgeya, shines in its manly display, full of pride like Śikhaṇḍin.
Even the sovereign of the gods, having disregarded the nectar of immortality, longs for the honey from the bimba-fruit-like lower lip of a young woman as it emerges from the opening of her garment.
She sports among the many flowers upon the honey-scented ear-ornaments of the young women and the crest-jewels of the youths,
like a female bee amidst the blossoms of the forest.
First a spreading bashfulness, followed by gestures nourished by the emotions and sentiments of love— like an actress after emerging from behind the curtain, this beloved captivates the mind.
The passion placed upon you by the fair-limbed woman was like turmeric applied to a cloth;
it was suddenly washed away by that slanderer, as if by falling water.
O deer, because you are harassed by tigers blinded by passion for the fragrance spreading in all directions,
there is no place anywhere for you even if you take up residence near the [sandalwood] navel.
There is a distinction between the *vaṭa*, *kuṭaja*, *śāla*, *śālmali*, *rasāla*, *bahu-sāra*, and *sindhu-vāra* trees,
even though they share an equality in fragrance produced by the Malaya mountains.
Having abandoned Śaṅkara— who possesses millions of matted locks— due to the fault of fickleness,
O Jāhnavī, you now roll along the banks of Prayāga while following a single banyan tree.
The night knows the meeting and the parting of its four watches,
just as a female tortoise knows both the contraction and the extension of her limbs.
O fortunate one, as her friend’s glance enters through a gap in the enclosure to behold you,
it captivates you like an arrow of the God of Love lodged within the cage of your youthful heart.
O you who are skilled in discernment, do not count him as being equal to a merchant's scale;
for this Dharma-jar outweighs the light and lifts the heavy to the top.
The sky is traversable by Anuru in a single day, the earth is but a single step for Vāmana, and even the ocean can be crossed by boat; with what, then, can we compare the minds of the virtuous?

O gazelle-eyed one, the stars shine in the sky like a multitude of leaf-letters clearly visible upon the lap of the goddess of fortune, who is marked by streaks of black soot in the form of widespread darkness.

The teacher of the god of love, acting as a preceptor, makes his young novice dance upon the bed according to the modes of sexual union, using various graceful bodily movements like a slender cane-staff.
Even though this pleasure of yours is contrary [to dharma], it is like the current of a river flowing with the slope;
it sweeps away my heart, along with its very roots, by its force, like a tree on a riverbank.
Even the criticism directed at those who possess great power is placed on the very side of their ornamentation;
the followers of Kaṇāda proclaim [only] their own heat, unrighteousness, and hatred.
O friend, whom do the wicked and the side-long glances of courtesans not deceive? Both are crooked, deceitfully affectionate, soiled, and they cling close to the ear.
O beloved, hailstones emerge from the belly of the cloud-pot encircled by flashes of lightning,
stealing the luster of pure white rice while accompanied by water.
O housewife, what is the use of services such as fanning for me, a traveler on the desert road?
For my asceticism finds its peace within the pair of plantain-tree trunks that are your thighs.
For even when performed with deficiency, an action executed by a great person results in beauty;
the dance of a woman with full hips captivates the heart, even though it is slowed by the weight of her heavy buttocks.
Seeing that single line marked with her own name in the counting of virtuous women, the young men were able only to laugh; they themselves were not able to restrain it.
Your body, like the Vindhya mountain, with its slopes possessing various whirlpools of the Narmadā,
obstructs the movement even of a sage, as it is capable of paralyzing the chariot of the sun.

O wicked bull, who breaks through the enclosure, who endures being struck down, who delights excessively in unrestrained misconduct, and who is lustful for hundreds of others' fields— do you even remember your own home?
The support of its frame, the extent of its threads, and the degree of its sagging— all these serve only for the destruction of one who sleeps within its fold, whether it be a net or a wicked man.
Upon the peak of the Vindhya mountain, the wind— acting as a sword for the rows of clouds—
shatters them with the rising light of lightning, solely for the purpose of slaying the travelers.
First washed by tears— the dust shaken from her hanging braids—
and subsequently by water, is the footprint of my wife as she arrived home.
While you were sleeping on my chest, you did not touch my head to place it upon my face during our exhaustion from lovemaking,
as you were held far away by the weight of your full and lofty breasts.
O messenger, by bringing him under your influence through the employment of your speech,
you are the fang of that libertine, intended for the destruction of virtuous women.
Thus ends the Section on the Letter *Va*, accompanied by the commentary *Vibhāvya*. Now begins the Section on the Letter *Śa*:
By him who, through his expertise in enchantment, has mastered even the Goddess Śrī within the coils of the serpent;
If even that Hari is a person, then what can we do about other persons as well?
I suspect: what young man could possibly move you, who are like a slab of pride and consist of such steadfastness that you paralyze even the arms of the God of Love?
Though fashioned from the hardest gold, fragile as a tiger’s claw,
you too dwell in the hearts of even the most foolish among the young.
O slender-limbed one, as soon as it is heard, your voice—captivating to the ear—dwells upon the throat with an intensity of passion;
yet, though you are as sweet as a song, your body does not grasp the meaning [of your words].
The Goddess of Fortune obtained a kingdom through a *śrīphala* fruit due to its slight resemblance to a king;
yet, because of the perfect resemblance of two jars to breasts, a jar attained the status of a universal monarch (*cakravartin*).
The hips upon the ground, the beloved in the lap, fear in the mind, the crown upon the husband’s arm,
and silent breath in the mouth— if such is this lovemaking, then heaven is but a blade of grass.
As if embracing, as if kissing, as if gazing, and as if scraping her, insatiable and as if holding it within my heart, I remember her hips again and again.
O fair-faced one, having dealt him a blow to the head with your foot, let that serpent be driven away by you,
even though he bears the mark of the discus, like Kāliya was from the Yamunā.
Worthy of pity indeed is that slender-limbed woman, whether she be full of prosperity or full of virtue,
for she has been abandoned by you— who are otherwise subject only to affection— just as a wick is cast off by a lamp.
Like a parrot in a cage of wooden rods, growing day by day,
this grief with its sharp-pointed shafts like those of the God of Love cuts through the heart of my beloved.
Having heard of the sudden death of his son, that parrot— the sole repository of all wonders—
a traveler, upon his very arrival, recognized the loss of his wife’s modesty.
Though the earth, encircled by the coils of the serpent Śeṣa, was lifted up by Kṛṣṇa with his chest, it is still called "immovable" (Acala); for what indeed is impossible for the Earth?
Alas, this dark girl, captivating the mind with her glances,
destroys her former husband just as a creeping vine of smoke obscures a painting on a wall.
I remember her on the day of her departure: her departing hundreds of times, her returning hundreds of times, her clutching my neck hundreds of times, and her saying "I am going" hundreds of times.
Questioned by the cowherd women whose voices were nourished by the sound of what they had heard, Kṛṣṇa,
with his eyes fixed upon their breasts, expressed his consent through the humming of his flute.
O crescent moon, do not harbor pride on the grounds that your foot has been placed upon the head of Śaṅkara;
for your reward shall be the cleansing of the dust from Caṇḍī’s feet.
Upon the treetop, a pair of birds dwells, content in their nest swaying in the breeze; they find solace in their unceasing play, regarding only their own actions as refuge and disregarding all fear.
O parrot, the Nārada of the battle of amorous love, the sole essence of the heart’s secret, the omniscient one;
O you who are silent in the presence of your elders, be gracious and split open the rose-apple fruit!
O Rudra, you carry matted locks upon your head, yet even after weeping, you acquire silver;
who knows the true nature of you who possess half of this belly?
O Ketakī, surrounded as you are by wicked serpents, you are indeed to be heard of like nectar and seen from afar like a digit of the moon, but you are certainly not to be touched by us.
O messenger, having bowed and offered flowers endowed with qualities brought forth by my hearing,
I have been brought under your control, as if by the creeper of Love’s bow.
O Śākhoṭaka, Śākhoṭaja, Vaikhānasa, Karaṭa, and Pūjya, cry out for a long time!
O calculators, you have no place here of respect; you alone are the authoritative person.
O you whose beauty is like a crescent moon, as you proceed to take the hand of another,
the splendor of your limbs brings shame to the beauty of a doll made from the sword of Love.
Even when maintained with laxity, those of good conduct do not abandon their master's work;
though their arms are pulled by force, their bracelets jingle and run along.
Thus ends the section on the letter *śa*, accompanied by its commentary.
The section on the letter *ṣa*:
Having abandoned the weapon [the lotus] which is inhabited by six-legged insects and filled with pollen-beetles;
Now Śiva bears you as his spear, with a waist that can be grasped by a single fist.

Thus ends the Section on the Letter *Ṣa*, accompanied by the commentary *Vibhāvya*. ********************************************************** The Section on the Letter *Sa*: She is merely a housewife, whose designation is the performance of duties appropriate for the day.
At night, you are to be served like the subsequent lunar day following the second day.
The multitude of sweat-drops clinging to the fresh nail-marks on your breasts shines as if it were a stream of pearls entering a silk thread.
Let one female elephant, who dwells between two exceedingly tall bulls blinded by rut, possess the pride of good fortune as the ornament of the herd.
O fortunate one, having been humbled by the pain in my head— inflicted by your foot— which I inferred from the pain in your own feet, I have come here myself to appease you, O offender.
What does a sesame oil presser gain by using a wheel when he merely extracts oil?
But he who moves even kings is truly a potter, and indeed a master of the wheel.
O simple one, you do not know that the course of unchaste women’s glances— like rivers— is full of many breakages, many flavors, and many turnings, despite their being full of passion.
O friend, the shadow of the tree, oppressed by the rows of rays from the midday sun,
takes refuge at the base of the tree on all sides, as if to plunge into the water of its basin.
"Friend, listen: this beloved of mine asks about the cities, villages, and rivers along the very path by which he came, as if he were asking others who had arrived together with him."
In the evening, the sun enters the fire; that fire, the arrow of Love; and that arrow, the heart of a woman separated from her beloved;
this heart, too, enters the mass of darkness; and that darkness, in turn, enters the sky to its full extent.
Resembling a conch shell filled for the occasion of the battle of love, with its neck-stalk doubly swollen,
it warbles a sweet sound atop the ruined palace like one desiring victory.
This weeping— with quivering lips, incessant tears, and breasts trembling from the suppression of sound—
with the face resting upon hands placed on the knees, belongs to one of a gentle nature.
May the crane-woman, who nourishes her beloved hidden in the nest with food brought by herself and who knows the flavor of innate love, carry away the pride of the fortunate woman.
For backbiters who grasp with their own natural juice and prick with heaps of thorns when taking hold,
even the expansion of their sheaths is untrustworthy— just like jackfruit trees.
Hara taught young women that their charm does not arise from courtesy,
as he placed only the left half of the Goddess into the design of his own body.
O fortunate one, that slender-limbed woman, having been crushed and oppressed by you against the wall of her own chamber,
lives only through that very suffering, harboring a deep hatred for physicians.
She, composed of virtues, naturally pure, and of slender form, has been whirled around by you— who know many mantras— like a saffron garland, now dependent upon the grasping of your hand.
O beautiful one, fortunate with your modest smile, as you move away slightly as if merely touched,
the more you touch my heart.
O friend, the beloved, having gained the opportunity, brings as much happiness as the husband never can;
even from an unobstructed breeze, the air from a window becomes cool.

O friend, with your face perpetually flushed, you swallow the string of your words as if they were poison; disregarding both medicine and mantras, O serpent-like woman, you cause your lover to turn away from you.
On the bank of the lotus pond, the female water-snake, with her body as lovely as a land-lotus and standing on one leg with her other foot marked by a wound,
comforts a small fish.

Having exposed her navel-base, which is exceptionally fair and marked with nail-scratches, and being naked, O Wind, have you been served by her? Have you committed suicide by leaping from the Malaya cliff?
Casting herself with all her limbs upon the bed, the fickle Goddess of Fortune favors even a weary and indolent man who is fortunate, just as she does one who exerts himself in love.
That very night is well-spent when, repeatedly recalling the sorrows of separation,
she embraces him firmly again and again at the beginning of the night.
Just as a female servant performs her service with inner fear,
so too does his wife perform it with apprehension, jealousy, and dread.
O beautiful one, just as her friend displays the beauty of your rival,
so does my gaze fall upon her with envy, for I am your sole servant.

"O friend, this entire village has been made to resound with cries of 'Fortunate one! Fortunate one! by her, who spends her days sleeping while her lower lip is wounded by nail-marks and adorned with decorative leaf-patterns—all under her own control."
Like rivers that dry up at his house, the women born of noble lineages wither away;
he finds satisfaction only in salty waves, like a cloud over the ocean.
O fierce one, whose heart has become as hard as a stylus, who alone adorns the entire army, and who possesses tusks like mountain peaks— I believe your mind, O Giribhū, has become like realgar.
O friend, your anger— difficult to fathom and dense, causing displeasure even toward those who are dear— stands upon your downcast face like a wicked man, hard to perceive.
Having bathed with her clothes on while perspiring, Manoharā, walking seven steps across seven circles,
bows down in shame, trembling with the agitation of love's fire.
This assembly of those with equal conduct,
proceeding with great excellence, has been shattered by those of discordant conduct upon their arrival, like a poetic composition ruined by a flawed section.
O friend, the sexual union of all women is indeed captivating like milk;
yet that of her alone, through repeated recurrence, is as sweet as fresh cream.
Though she does not leave you even in dreams, and though she dwells within your heart as one who favors you,
you do not perceive her secret transgressions, just as one fails to recognize a corrupt intellect.
O lady of faultless limbs, like a whirlwind moving with its revolutions, you seize the mind as it were a blade of grass;
you carry it away, cast it down, make it tremble, cause it to wander, weigh it down, and bring it to fall.

O gambler, it is the same to you whether she is a woman possessing many auspicious marks or merely a woman; for in the rules of gambling, whether it be ten million or a single cowrie shell, everything is equally a stake.
Afflicted by the fire of separation, that poor woman lives on even though she dies again and again;
like a *śārī* bird, O rogue, she has been won over by you through the casting of a favorable die.
From his touch alone he produces perspiration, yet he does not grant me sleep;
like a lover, the summer heat does not tolerate even for a moment my garment upon my hips.

O handsome one, through meditation upon you, that young woman bears the fruit of her mind-born passion— which was previously contrary to the [proper] time— just as a fresh creeper bears fruit through the power of its longing for the sap of a beautiful tree.
She touches him with her nails but does not scratch his garment; she grasps him but does not release him;
she does not let go, nor does she yield to passion; she passes the night without sleeping.
O friend, my sidelong glance, having bypassed her waist, does not leave her pair of breasts and hips,
just as a crow at a sacred bathing place does not leave the two banks of a river.
My beloved, reproaching me with a bashful smile and gentle sighs, saying "Do not touch me," became indignant and remained there having closed the window.

Her sexual union—with its grasping of the hand, its weeping, its reproaches, its clutching with fingernails and fists, and its desire for victory—is true *surata*; any other is merely a *prājāpatya* sacrifice.
O friend, those who are themselves impure do not utter even the name of the pure;
by whom has it ever been heard that the cuckoos produce any sound other than "kuhu"?
Those mountains which were cast into the ocean by Rāma’s forces as being "very small" have indeed remained steadfast; alas, their great pride was due to nothing but their own insignificance!

That dark-complexioned, slender-limbed woman, scorched by the intense heat of separation from her lover— a heat more piercing than any cooling remedy— has been reduced to paleness, like a blade of *dūrvā* grass withered by the frost.
O friend, she did not become so intoxicated when sprinkled with the water from the stream held steadily and carefully in my hand, as she did when seen by me trembling.
"O friend, O devoted wife who has rendered Cupid powerless, who pays you any heed?
Have you not heard that even the venerable Hara was pierced by that very Kāma?"
She has no sense of me as a slave, nor affection, nor even shame, nor trust;
alas, having gazed upon her newly wedded bride, I think we have become [mere] fuel for the fire.
This clever housewife, having enjoyed him at night when he returned after a long time,
does not show her own body with its white nail-marks still moist with saffron at the break of day.

O beloved, you who were once so devoted to my breasts, hips, and thighs, clinging closely and full of affection, it is now the ripening of time that you have grown indifferent, like a nail-mark on the body.
Lacking luster night after night, that fair-limbed woman lies upon a bed cold with much frost;
from the separation from you, she burns like a medicinal herb on the slopes of the Himalayas.
O handsome one, that friend of yours enters your passionless heart but does not emerge; she finds no stability there, like a streak of frost upon the orb of the sun.
O crescent moon, what indeed has not been proclaimed by the very capture of the hare— your delicacy, your luster, your extreme gentleness, and your inner virtues?

Let there be no distinction for those whose minds are intent solely on fragrance; nevertheless, for those seeking merit, the *aśvattha* tree is to be sought out for the sake of worship, just as the sandalwood tree is.
Just as a housewife massages her sleeping husband or fans him while he lies there,
so too does she provide consolation to the youth by fixing her gaze through the opening in the house wall.
It is true that she is stubborn toward those of meager virtues;
yet, O handsome one, when it comes to a serpent of equal [skill], she bows down with her tip offered up, like the staff of Śiva’s bow.
Having made her full of tears like the all-enduring earth,
your great love has now transferred itself into the form of the interior of your dwelling.
Indeed, protection is not possible for those who are passionate and whose conduct is inherently fickle;
even upon the head of Hara, the Gaṅgā suffers the embrace of serpents.
While lotus filaments, *ketaka*, mango, and jasmine flowers are easily available, the female bee,
blinded by desire, longs for the state of being the string upon the bow of Love.
The co-wife was ashamed, the lover was angry and afraid, and the friend was comforted when the physicians diagnosed the young woman's suffering as being caused by staying awake.

Under the pretext of massaging him who has returned after a very long time, the housewife embraces him limb by limb; she indulges in the display of jealous pride and thus brings her longing to fruition.
She is red in every way, yet she does not bear passion upon her face as a *guñjā* berry does;
your passion, O eloquent speaker, resides only in your mouth like that of a parrot.
In the evening, having fallen between the arms of her lover and spent the entire night in amorous play,
the young woman is ridiculed by her friends at dawn as she offers him a lamp.
O messenger, that fire of sharp pride is difficult to cook with great affection; yet, making you like a ladle, I have placed my trust in you.
The loss of ichor, the desire for victory, and the battle that ends only with the loss of life— what calamity does this not spread, O tusker, through your youth-exuberant state?
When the parrot speaks to the charming girl, her lover departs from his seat, her friend laughs, the young woman enters the house as if it were the earth,
the rival wife burns with jealousy, and [the husband] becomes pleased.
O Snow, by your grace, I enjoy my beloved— who has her limbs drawn together, whose garment is doubled over, and whose passion quivers in her mind alone— as if she were a simple girl.
O friend, though you dwell eternally within his great heart, which is filled with aesthetic flavor (rasa),
you do not attain even the slightest moisture, like the submarine fire within the ocean.
O friend, having concealed even the joy of the moon's rising and so forth, this very day at its conclusion— like a fruitless final day of a festival— torments me like a cold winter day.
In the abode of the gods, two youths, whose eyes and hearts were drawn to one another,
offered each other flowers that they had gathered for the purpose of worshipping the deity.
In the evening, the sound of bees emerging from within the lotuses is like a cry of lamentation uttered by the day-lotuses, despondent at the loss of their friend.
Although I myself had created this great cause for her wrath,
she fell weeping upon my very chest, her thighs trembling, even though she was among her friends.
"O fortunate one, even this companion of mine has her arms grown languid from fanning you;
do not move away just a little, lest my friend's ritual of anointing with fragrant unguents remain unfinished."
This newly wedded bride, who was bashful during the application of nails and teeth and deeply resentful,
has now become one who can only be won over by much entreaty and the grasping of her feet through anger.

Whom do they not terrify— whether they be men or arrows— when their dark wings (or feathers) are well-grasped, when they are light, capable of piercing others, exceedingly sharp, and yet fallen from the string (or virtue)?
The very cause of intoxication, manifested by their own temples,
made both the rut-fluid of the elephant and the gift of the wicked man truly identical in effect.
It is true that her husband was unskilled, yet she herself was expert in the art of lovemaking;
by means of her own ingenuity, Ekalavya acquired a clay model of his teacher’s bow.
Having been treated with contempt by you, that man of good fortune has been brought to humiliation;
he spreads his own pallor of separation, which resembles a bath in ashes.
“Friend, you shall send me much karanja oil with your message,” so addressed,
the unfaithful woman restrains the tears that have welled up upon meeting her father-in-law’s house.

O beautiful one, in the pervasive darkness where there is no distinction, the flame of the crest-jewel serves as a lamp for unchaste women, appearing like the wick that reveals the path of the serpent.
The entire forest is shrouded by a mass of grass; the moon, the sun, and the stars have turned yellow;
and the paths are obscured as a dark cloud rises up.
When a matter that is not yet properly established is made clear by oneself in haste,
it remains defective, just like the first son of Vinatā.
For knowledge indeed becomes beautiful only in a virtuous person; in a wicked person, it is fruitless.
A vulture is not sought after by anyone on account of its far-reaching vision.
People call him fortunate, saying he has his own husband; this does not please me, for even ambrosia becomes distasteful when it is presented as medicine.
For even from her palace window, his gaze— though he had exerted himself to remain steady— carried him away,
just as the Ganges falling from the peak of the Snowy Mountain carries away Airāvata.
O slender-limbed one, she who dwells with me in the heat is my retinue; of this there is no doubt.
Yet, clinging to me, she does not bring me comfort, like the shadow of a parasol on a cold day.
O sole abode of all virtues, by dwelling among the Dānavas you have become a king of trees upon the earth, whose fruits and flowers are unacceptable even to the virtuous.
O beautiful one, upon your ear, which bears an earring like a discus,
falls the exceedingly sharp arrow of your sidelong glance, ever fond of Arjuna.
The abundance of fruit is indeed within one's own control, and the towering shade is there for the people to subsist upon;
for a virtuous man, like a tree in a desert, merely the capacity to sustain life is to be desired.
O friend, the prosperity of a wicked person spreads far and wide in order to produce distress, delusion, and trembling, and even to destroy living beings, just like a fever.
Fortune does not protect even a slight familiarity once she has been made excessively comfortable, like a courtesan;
likewise, the Goddess of Speech does not abandon one even after birth after birth, like a wicked mistress.
O friend, having merely seen a lotus pond with newly sprouted leaves near his own dwelling, my husband, crying out "Alas, my wife! upon his long-awaited return, has fallen [unconscious].
Even though he never shows any aversion anywhere due to his four-faced nature,
he is nonetheless as truly single-hearted toward his beloved as Brahmā himself.
He is truly sweet, certainly clever, and surely a possessor of artistic skill;
yet, like the spotless moon on the first day of the lunar fortnight, he knows no second woman.
Like Mount Maināka, the virtuous person, intent on protecting his own side, may even depart from his own place, sink into the ocean, or resort to the lowly.

"Restrain the flow of tears, my friend; anoint your eyes with collyrium and put on these bracelets, so that your beloved may behold at once the luster of both your sprout-like arms and your lotus-like face."
She, with her limbs pale and weak, goes wherever you lead her;
like a stylus, she is for you—knower of deception—to be mastered merely by the grasp of the hand.
O lotus-faced friend, like the fortune of a miser, you— who are despised by the whole world—
are for this old man useful only for guarding and looking after [your person].
Thus ends the section on the letter *sa*, accompanied by its commentary.
Now follows the section on the letter *ha*:
A certain discordant cooing was heard from the window by a friend who understands the heart's secrets.
O fair-limbed one, that you come to me under the pretext of fear, though your bed has been broken by our quarrel.
"O friend, this thread of collyrium applied with a probe captivates the heart;
O charming girl, it is like a scar scarified by the brow-bow of the one who discharges the arrows of his eyes."
Laughing, you were kicked from the bed by a blow of my foot and lay upon the ground;
yet, O beloved, even when such an unseemly thing was done, you did not depart from my heart.
The co-wife laughs, the mother-in-law weeps, and her friends cover their faces with their hands as she,
in her dream-like state, prattles your name, O fortunate one.
O friend, this powerful grief for my beloved, which exerts its activity at every moment, will tear apart my heart just as a streak of water breaks a water-jar.
Alas! This separation, with its irresistible and intense agitation, burns me on all sides;
yet, like the dawn that warms the sun-stone, it does not reduce me to ashes.
Having been swept away by your waves, O river, and whirled in circles until cast into destruction,
the tree was abandoned by you in the sky, stripped of its fruit, leaves, and bark.
On the posterior of her hips, from which the binding of the creeper-like girdle has been removed after being enjoyed by another lover,
the line of body hair shines forth like a streak of venom on the breast of Śambhu.

Thus ends the Section on the Letter *Ha*, accompanied by its analytical commentary. The Section on the Letter *Kṣa*: Since milk possesses a state of endearment even when it has attained a tranquil appearance, [it is like the Buddha].
The mountain bends its limbs like the remnants of a fever from love.
Forgiven is your being cast out, since you lie there fast asleep with your feet tucked up;
why do you open your thighs with hot sighs that make them bristle?

The pungency of that which arises from something base and its intense intoxication, as well as the greatness and lightness of honey and a petty man respectively, serve to distinguish them. [This work],
whose style differs from the former masters— Guṇāḍhya, Bhavabhūti, Bāṇa, and the author of the *Raghuvaṃśa*— [is composed by me].
What fault is there if the virtuous look upon me, who am devoted to the Goddess of Speech?
To whom does a good poem and sweet speech not bring joy—a fresh subject matter possessing a true reflection, fit for presentation to a worthy recipient? (GAss 698)

The *Saptaśatī* is unique in its meter, second to none in its essence as the three worlds, distinguished by the skill of its lucid expression, beneficial to the five-arrowed god and the six-legged bee, and an ornament for the ear.
This composition, a lion’s roar in the battle of poets, a concordant repetition of the [Vedic] vowels, a dialogue with nectar alone, and a root of delight for the learned, has been created by me.
This *Saptaśatī* has been purified and illuminated by my two disciples and brothers, Udayana and Balabhadra, just as the sky is made bright by the sun and the moon.
The wise Govardhanācārya has composed this *Āryā-saptaśatī* for the constant delight of the best of poets, as a respectful salutation with joined palms at the feet of Hari.
Thus ends the *Āryā-saptaśatī* composed by Govardhanācārya.
